content.text:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

input.prompt:
You are generating ambitious project ideas for a 48-hour AI-agent hackathon called neatHack (by neatlogs), Oct 10-12 2026. This is a brainstorm; your returned text IS the deliverable (raw data for the orchestrator, not a message to a human).

THE CHALLENGE: one track. Build an AI agent that completes a substantial real task start to finish. Judges reward visible planning, tool use, state/memory, context handling, execution, recovery from failure, verification, iteration.

JUDGING (out of 100): the agent itself 30; use of the mandatory stack (neatlogs + Entire + cfo.ai) 25; demo video 20; building in public on X 15; usefulness and originality 10.

MANDATORY STACK (every project must use all three, with evidence) — design against these descriptions, do not re-research unless a specific integration detail matters:
- neatlogs: AI-agent observability/tracing. You instrument your agent so every run, tool call, decision and failure is a trace you can inspect and debug. Make traces central to how the agent is built and improved, not bolted on.
- Entire (hack.entire.io): agent checkpointing tied to a GitHub repo via a CLI, plus Trails/Graph/Brain features. Submission includes a checkpoint link + ID.
- cfo.ai: a business-planning agent (pricing, costs, revenue, runway). The resulting business plan goes in the submission; ideas where a real pricing/business model is intrinsic score better.
- Bonus (optional): Crustdata API, 5,000 free credits of company + people data (firmographics, people/contact enrichment).

CONSTRAINTS: solo builder, ~2 working days. Compute is ONE tiny AWS box: us-east-1 only, pre-set Hackathon_VPC only, only EC2 + Lambda + IAM + load balancers, ONE small EC2 instance (t2/t3/t3a nano-large), EBS <=50GB, total spend <=$25. No GPU, no training; heavy inference goes through hosted LLM APIs. Submission is a public GitHub repo + a demo video, announced by quote-tweeting neatlogs on X, so it must narrate well in public across 48h and show well on camera.

WHAT WINS: the agent does a SUBSTANTIAL end-to-end task autonomously with visible planning, recovery and verification (the 30%); the mandatory tools are INTRINSIC; there is ONE jaw-dropping demo moment on video (the 20%); a natural building-in-public arc on X (the 15%); shippable by one person in 48h on a tiny box. Be genuinely ambitious; avoid generic "chatbot for X" or "RAG over docs". Favour agents that take real actions and close a real loop with a crisp wow-moment.

YOUR LENS: consumer / prosumer life-admin. Everyday high-stakes personal tasks done fully end-to-end: insurance or billing disputes, refund/chargeback fights, benefits or tax paperwork, moving house, medical-bill negotiation, bureaucratic form marathons, booking/rebooking under constraints. The agent should navigate real portals, forms, emails and async comms, keep state across a multi-day process, recover when a step fails, and verify the task is actually done.

RETURN exactly 3 ideas, each in this exact format and nothing else:
### <Idea name>
- Pitch: <one sentence>
- The agent (30%): <the substantial end-to-end task, the loop, how it plans/recovers/verifies>
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): <the single strongest thing to show on video>
- Stack fit (25%): <how neatlogs tracing, Entire checkpoints and cfo.ai's business plan are intrinsic; Crustdata if relevant>
- Build-in-public hook (15%): <the arc / milestones that make good X posts>
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: <why one person can ship a real demo in time on a tiny box; the single biggest risk>
- Ambition: <why this is bold, not incremental>

Do not write files or make any changes. Return only the three ideas.

You are generating ambitious project ideas for a 48-hour AI-agent hackathon called neatHack (by neatlogs), Oct 10-12 2026. This is a brainstorm; your returned text IS the deliverable (raw data for the orchestrator, not a message to a human).

THE CHALLENGE: one track. Build an AI agent that completes a substantial real task start to finish. Judges reward visible planning, tool use, state/memory, context handling, execution, recovery from failure, verification, iteration.

JUDGING (out of 100): the agent itself 30; use of the mandatory stack (neatlogs + Entire + cfo.ai) 25; demo video 20; building in public on X 15; usefulness and originality 10.

MANDATORY STACK (every project must use all three, with evidence) — design against these descriptions, do not re-research unless a specific integration detail matters:
- neatlogs: AI-agent observability/tracing. You instrument your agent so every run, tool call, decision and failure is a trace you can inspect and debug. Make traces central to how the agent is built and improved, not bolted on.
- Entire (hack.entire.io): agent checkpointing tied to a GitHub repo via a CLI, plus Trails/Graph/Brain features. Submission includes a checkpoint link + ID.
- cfo.ai: a business-planning agent (pricing, costs, revenue, runway). The resulting business plan goes in the submission; ideas where a real pricing/business model is intrinsic score better.
- Bonus (optional): Crustdata API, 5,000 free credits of company + people data (firmographics, people/contact enrichment).

CONSTRAINTS: solo builder, ~2 working days. Compute is ONE tiny AWS box: us-east-1 only, pre-set Hackathon_VPC only, only EC2 + Lambda + IAM + load balancers, ONE small EC2 instance (t2/t3/t3a nano-large), EBS <=50GB, total spend <=$25. No GPU, no training; heavy inference goes through hosted LLM APIs. Submission is a public GitHub repo + a demo video, announced by quote-tweeting neatlogs on X, so it must narrate well in public across 48h and show well on camera.

WHAT WINS: the agent does a SUBSTANTIAL end-to-end task autonomously with visible planning, recovery and verification (the 30%); the mandatory tools are INTRINSIC; there is ONE jaw-dropping demo moment on video (the 20%); a natural building-in-public arc on X (the 15%); shippable by one person in 48h on a tiny box. Be genuinely ambitious; avoid generic "chatbot for X" or "RAG over docs". Favour agents that take real actions and close a real loop with a crisp wow-moment.

YOUR LENS: fintech / finance / business-ops where cfo.ai is NATIVE, not bolted on. The product itself is financial, so a real pricing/revenue/runway model is intrinsic. Push past: an agent that runs invoicing + collections end to end (dunning, negotiation, reconciliation); a spend-audit agent that finds and cancels waste across a company's SaaS/cloud bills and proves savings; a financial-close or bookkeeping agent that categorizes, reconciles and closes a period with an audit trail; a pricing-experiment agent that proposes, simulates and sets prices and tracks revenue impact; a fundraising/runway agent. Verification and audit trail matter a lot here (neatlogs = the audit log).

RETURN exactly 3 ideas, each in this exact format and nothing else:
### <Idea name>
- Pitch: <one sentence>
- The agent (30%): <the substantial end-to-end task, the loop, how it plans/recovers/verifies>
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): <the single strongest thing to show on video>
- Stack fit (25%): <how neatlogs tracing, Entire checkpoints and cfo.ai's business plan are intrinsic; Crustdata if relevant>
- Build-in-public hook (15%): <the arc / milestones that make good X posts>
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: <why one person can ship a real demo in time on a tiny box; the single biggest risk>
- Ambition: <why this is bold, not incremental>

Do not write files or make any changes. Return only the three ideas.

If the probe fails it does not loop blindly, it reads the trace of what it just tried, discards that hypothesis then moves to the next. It writes a postmortem with the timeline and the fix. <result>### DeFlake
- Pitch: An agent that hunts a repo's flaky tests, proves the flake statistically, isolates the nondeterminism and ships a fix that passes 100 out of 100 runs.
- The agent (30%): Point it at a real public repo with a "flaky" label backlog. It plans a campaign: pick a candidate test, run it in isolation N times and in randomized suite order N times to measure the true flake rate and classify the cause (ordering dependency on shared state, time or timezone, randomness without a seed, concurrency race, network or filesystem leak). It forms a hypothesis, writes the minimal fix (seed the RNG, freeze the clock, isolate the fixture, add a proper await or lock), re-runs the quarantined test 100x to confirm zero failures, then runs the full suite to confirm no regressions. Recovery is the core loop: when a hypothesis fails because the flake rate is unchanged, it reverts to its last checkpoint, records the falsified hypothesis in the trace and tries the next cause class. It opens a PR with before and after flake rates, the root-cause writeup and the reproduction command.
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): a live on-screen counter. The test runs 100 times before the fix and fails 7 times with red ticks piling up, the agent ships the one-line fix, then runs 100 times again and the counter climbs to 100/100 green with zero failures. Red wall to green wall in one cut.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs is the measurement the method depends on, since every one of the hundreds of test runs is a trace and the flake rate is computed from traces grouped by run, so observability is the instrument not decoration. Each hypothesis attempt is an Entire checkpoint tied to the repo, so a falsified fix reverts to the last green checkpoint and the Trail shows the dead ends it walked back from. cfo.ai models "DeFlake CI" priced per CI-hour saved, since a flaky suite burns reruns and engineer trust, modelling inference cost per flake against a per-repo subscription with free-tier repos converting to paid teams. Crustdata sizes the go-to-market by filtering companies on engineering headcount and public monorepo activity for the target list and TAM.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): milestone posts write themselves. Post 1, it found a test that fails 1 in 14 runs on a repo everyone knows. Post 2, the neatlogs trace classifying the cause as a shared-fixture leak. Post 3, the falsified first hypothesis and the walk-back. Post 4, 100/100 green and the PR link. A flake-rate number anchors every post.
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: one targeted test run many times is CPU-time bound but trivial for a small library, and the whole run is a Python or JS repo with a fast suite on one t3.small. The single biggest risk is picking a repo whose flake does not reproduce on the box, so pre-scout two or three repos with labeled flaky tests and sub-minute suites before the clock starts, and keep a seeded synthetic flaky repo as a fallback demo.
- Ambition: flaky tests are the most hated and least automated corner of CI, and a fix is only believable with statistical proof, so an agent that measures nondeterminism, reasons about its cause and proves the cure 100x is doing what most human engineers avoid and most bots cannot verify.

### Bisector
- Pitch: Give it a "worked in v1.2, broken now" report and it bisects the real commit history to the exact culprit, explains the root cause and ships a fix with a permanent regression test.
- The agent (30%): It takes a regression described against two refs, writes a failing reproduction from the report, then drives git bisect across the history between the good and bad ends. At each step it checks out the commit, builds, runs the reproduction and labels the commit good or bad, marking broken intermediate commits as skip and routing around them. Planning is explicit: it estimates the step count as log2 of the range and narrows to one commit. Having found the culprit it reads the diff, writes the root-cause explanation, authors the minimal fix plus the reproduction as a permanent regression test, confirms that test fails on the culprit and passes on the fix, then runs the full suite. Recovery shows up when a build fails mid-bisect or a step is ambiguous: it skips, re-anchors and continues rather than aborting.

- Build-in-public hook (15%): a countdown narrative. Post 1, a real regression nobody has located yet, range of 380 commits. Post 2, the live search collapsing, nine steps. ### SpeedPR
- Pitch: An agent that profiles a real library, rewrites a hot path and ships a PR with a measured speedup and the full test suite still green.

- Build-in-public hook (15%): a number people argue about. Post 1, the profile showing where a known library actually spends its time. Post 2, the optimization and why it is a complexity win not a micro-trick. Post 3, the honest benchmarking method on a burstable box, itself a thread engineers reply to. Post 4, the merged speedup and the table. A speedup multiplier is the most shareable artifact on X.
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: the agent, git and the suite run fine on one t3.small, and optimization work is CPU-light to produce. The single biggest risk is the box itself, since t2 and t3 are burstable so wall-clock is noisy, which is exactly why measurement leans on interleaved A and B sampling and a credit-independent counter and reports a confidence interval rather than a single wall-clock number, with a fallback of claiming only the complexity or allocation win if timing stays inside the noise.
- Ambition: an agent that optimizes code and then proves the optimization honestly, correctness and speed together, is doing the part of performance work that is hardest and most easily faked, and tying the business model directly to measured compute saved turns the demo number into the revenue model in one move.

<result>### DeFlake
- Pitch: An agent that hunts a repo's flaky tests, proves the flake statistically, isolates the nondeterminism and ships a fix that passes 100 out of 100 runs.
- The agent (30%): Point it at a real public repo with a "flaky" label backlog. It plans a campaign: pick a candidate test, run it in isolation N times and in randomized suite order N times to measure the true flake rate and classify the cause (ordering dependency on shared state, time or timezone, randomness without a seed, concurrency race, network or filesystem leak). It forms a hypothesis, writes the minimal fix (seed the RNG, freeze the clock, isolate the fixture, add a proper await or lock), re-runs the quarantined test 100x to confirm zero failures, then runs the full suite to confirm no regressions. Recovery is the core loop: when a hypothesis fails because the flake rate is unchanged, it reverts to its last checkpoint, records the falsified hypothesis in the trace and tries the next cause class. It opens a PR with before and after flake rates, the root-cause writeup and the reproduction command.
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): a live on-screen counter. The test runs 100 times before the fix and fails 7 times with red ticks piling up, the agent ships the one-line fix, then runs 100 times again and the counter climbs to 100/100 green with zero failures. Red wall to green wall in one cut.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs is the measurement the method depends on, since every one of the hundreds of test runs is a trace and the flake rate is computed from traces grouped by run, so observability is the instrument not decoration. Each hypothesis attempt is an Entire checkpoint tied to the repo, so a falsified fix reverts to the last green checkpoint and the Trail shows the dead ends it walked back from. cfo.ai models "DeFlake CI" priced per CI-hour saved, since a flaky suite burns reruns and engineer trust, modelling inference cost per flake against a per-repo subscription with free-tier repos converting to paid teams. Crustdata sizes the go-to-market by filtering companies on engineering headcount and public monorepo activity for the target list and TAM.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): milestone posts write themselves. Post 1, it found a test that fails 1 in 14 runs on a repo everyone knows. Post 2, the neatlogs trace classifying the cause as a shared-fixture leak. Post 3, the falsified first hypothesis and the walk-back. Post 4, 100/100 green and the PR link. A flake-rate number anchors every post.
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: one targeted test run many times is CPU-time bound but trivial for a small library, and the whole run is a Python or JS repo with a fast suite on one t3.small. The single biggest risk is picking a repo whose flake does not reproduce on the box, so pre-scout two or three repos with labeled flaky tests and sub-minute suites before the clock starts, and keep a seeded synthetic flaky repo as a fallback demo.
- Ambition: flaky tests are the most hated and least automated corner of CI, and a fix is only believable with statistical proof, so an agent that measures nondeterminism, reasons about its cause and proves the cure 100x is doing what most human engineers avoid and most bots cannot verify.

### Bisector
- Pitch: Give it a "worked in v1.2, broken now" report and it bisects the real commit history to the exact culprit, explains the root cause and ships a fix with a permanent regression test.
- The agent (30%): It takes a regression described against two refs, writes a failing reproduction from the report, then drives git bisect across the history between the good and bad ends. At each step it checks out the commit, builds, runs the reproduction and labels the commit good or bad, marking broken intermediate commits as skip and routing around them. Planning is explicit: it estimates the step count as log2 of the range and narrows to one commit. Having found the culprit it reads the diff, writes the root-cause explanation, authors the minimal fix plus the reproduction as a permanent regression test, confirms that test fails on the culprit and passes on the fix, then runs the full suite. Recovery shows up when a build fails mid-bisect or a step is ambiguous: it skips, re-anchors and continues rather than aborting.
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): the bisect runs live and the search space collapses on screen, 380 commits narrowed to one in nine steps, landing on a single commit, and the agent quotes the one line in that diff that caused the break and shows its new regression test going red on that commit and green on the fix.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs renders the bisect as a trace tree where every checkout, build and verdict is a span, so the search itself is the observability story and a failed build is a visible recovered span. Entire checkpoints anchor the good and bad ends and every skipped commit, so the agent jumps the working tree between checkpoints instead of re-cloning and the Graph shows the collapsing search. cfo.ai models "Bisector on-call" priced per incident resolved or per debugging-hour saved, since a human bisect of a large history is hours of senior time, modelling compute cost per build-step against a per-seat on-call subscription. Crustdata builds the target list from companies with large fast-moving repos and sizable on-call rotations.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): a countdown narrative. Post 1, a real regression nobody has located yet, range of 380 commits. Post 2, the live search collapsing, nine steps. Post 3, the culprit commit and the one offending line. Post 4, the PR with the fix and a regression test that can never silently return. Each post carries a shrinking number.
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: feasible if the target builds and tests fast, so choose a pure-language library whose suite runs in seconds and cap the bisect to a few hundred commits. One t3.small handles sequential checkouts and builds, and git bisect is standard tooling the agent only has to drive. The single biggest risk is build time per step on a heavy project, so pick a lightweight repo, bound the range and verify the reproduction is deterministic before starting the bisect.
- Ambition: autonomous root-cause location over history is a task agents almost never close end to end, because it needs a real plan, dozens of build-and-test cycles, recovery around broken commits and a verifiable fix, so doing it live on a public repo in front of judges is a serious claim about agent autonomy not a toy.

### SpeedPR
- Pitch: An agent that profiles a real library, rewrites a hot path and ships a PR with a measured speedup and the full test suite still green.
- The agent (30%): It runs the repo's benchmark or builds a micro-benchmark around a hot function, profiles to find the dominant cost, and forms an optimization hypothesis grounded in a complexity or allocation change rather than a guess (replace an O(n squared) scan with a hashed lookup, hoist an allocation out of a loop, memoize a pure call, batch IO). It implements the change, proves correctness by running the full suite green, then measures the speedup with an honest protocol: interleaved A and B sampling run back to back many times so burstable-CPU drift cancels, median with a confidence interval, plus a credit-independent counter like instruction count or allocations so the win does not rest on wall-clock alone. Recovery is intrinsic: if the suite breaks or the speedup lands inside the noise, it reverts to the checkpoint, records the null result in the trace and tries the next hot path. It opens a PR with a before and after table and the benchmark method.
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): a single before and after frame. Same function, same inputs, old path at 1.0x and new path at 2.4x with a tight confidence interval, and right beside it the full test suite going green, so the speedup and the correctness land in the same shot. The number is the hook and the green suite proves it is not cheating.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs holds every benchmark sample as a trace, so the median and confidence interval are computed from traced runs and the honest-measurement protocol lives in the observability layer by construction. Entire checkpoints the baseline and each optimization attempt, so a reverted change that fell inside the noise is a visible walked-back checkpoint on the Trail and the kept win is one clean step. cfo.ai models the most intrinsic business of the three: SpeedPR takes a share of the cloud bill it reduces, so the plan is a direct function of measured compute saved, modelling inference cost per optimization against revenue share on realized savings with a floor subscription. Crustdata sizes it by finding companies running large compute bills and heavy OSS dependencies for the target list and TAM.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): a number people argue about. Post 1, the profile showing where a known library actually spends its time. Post 2, the optimization and why it is a complexity win not a micro-trick. Post 3, the honest benchmarking method on a burstable box, itself a thread engineers reply to. Post 4, the merged speedup and the table. A speedup multiplier is the most shareable artifact on X.
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: the agent, git and the suite run fine on one t3.small, and optimization work is CPU-light to produce. The single biggest risk is the box itself, since t2 and t3 are burstable so wall-clock is noisy, which is exactly why measurement leans on interleaved A and B sampling and a credit-independent counter and reports a confidence interval rather than a single wall-clock number, with a fallback of claiming only the complexity or allocation win if timing stays inside the noise.
- Ambition: an agent that optimizes code and then proves the optimization honestly, correctness and speed together, is doing the part of performance work that is hardest and most easily faked, and tying the business model directly to measured compute saved turns the demo number into the revenue model in one move.

result: 3 OSS-maintainer agent ideas for neatHack (DeFlake 100/100-run flaky-test fix, Bisector live git-bisect regression hunter, SpeedPR proven-speedup optimizer), each verification-native and live on a real public repo, with intrinsic neatlogs/Entire/cfo.ai fit, a crisp wow number, and the burstable-box risk named per idea.</result>

It forms hypotheses ranked by evidence (bad tool arg vs missing context vs wrong plan vs flaky dependency), picks the narrowest fix on a bounded change surface (the system prompt, one tool's JSON schema, one guard/retry config or a single function), applies it, re-runs the exact failing input plus a smoke set then gates on a verifier that must independently pass before the patch is accepted. If the re-run still fails it rolls back and tries the next hypothesis, capping attempts so it cannot thrash. Planning is visible (a hypothesis board), recovery is the whole point (rollback plus next hypothesis), verification is a hard gate not a vibe.

Right, Mechanic reads the trace, narrates "the tool returned the invoice total as a string so the sum silently concatenated," edits the tool schema, re-runs and the same input now goes green, all autonomously, in one unbroken take. Biggest risk: the patch loop oscillating or producing a cosmetic fix that games the verifier, mitigated by a narrow change surface, an independent verifier on held-out inputs and a hard attempt cap with rollback.

### Scar
- Pitch: Every time an agent fails, this agent turns that exact failure into a permanent replayable regression test, growing an eval suite from real neatlogs traces so the same break can never ship twice.

On any failure or flagged bad output it reconstructs a deterministic test case from the trace: the input, the recorded tool returns kept as stubs and an assertion for what correct looked like (or the human's one-click "this was wrong"). It de-duplicates against existing cases by semantic signature so the suite grows in coverage not in noise, names and files the test then runs the whole suite against the current agent. The closing move is a bisect: when a case that once passed starts failing, Scar walks the Entire checkpoints to find which change regressed it and reports the culprit. Planning shows as the triage of which traces deserve to become tests, recovery as handling flaky non-deterministic steps by pinning seeds and replaying recorded tool returns, verification as the suite itself being the arbiter.

Entire is load-bearing twice: the checkpoints are both the timeline Scar bisects across to localize a regression and the two-point snapshot the submission shows. cfo.ai models eval-coverage-as-a-service: priced per agent and per retained test with trace ingestion as COGS, upsell on bisect and CI gating, which is a real defensible line. ### Crucible
- Pitch: A red-team agent that attacks another agent until it breaks, captures each exploit as a neatlogs trace, then hardens the target against that exact exploit and re-runs the attack to prove the hole is closed.

Every attempt is a neatlogs trace, so a success is a trace that shows the exploit landing (a planted fake secret read, a budget meter drained, a disallowed action taken). The hardener reads the winning traces, classifies the failure mode and installs the narrowest guard (input sanitizer, tool allowlist, loop ceiling, budget cap, output check), then the adversary re-runs the SAME attack to confirm it now fails and keeps mutating to find the next crack. The hardener reads that trace, writes a guard and the identical attack is replayed and bounces off. Same input, secret stays put, budget holds. The arms-race graph of generations sits on screen behind it.

Entire checkpoints each hardening generation, turning the arms race into a Trail and Graph you can walk; the submission checkpoint shows the agent at "vulnerable" and "hardened" with IDs. cfo.ai models agent-security-as-a-service: priced per agent audited and per hardening run with a managed continuous-hardening tier, which matches a real urgent buyer. Quote-tweet neatlogs: "I built an agent that jailbreaks other agents, then an agent that patches the jailbreak, live for 48h." - Ambition: It runs a live arms race between two agents and lets the defender win in real time, automating both halves of security work that is almost entirely manual today. Watching an agent close its own vulnerability on camera is a new thing to see.

I have more than enough to cut a strong top 10, so I'm synthesizing now rather than blocking on it. I did not kill it, and I can fold its ideas in or resume it if you want the healthcare/legal/insurance angle.

## What actually wins neatHack
The rubric rewards two things that are hard to fake: neatlogs being load-bearing (the 25%) and a demo moment that can't be staged (the 20%). The sharpest ideas are ones where the agent reads its own traces to decide what to do next, so the tool is the instrument, not a logging bolt-on. One strategic fork to hold in mind: the host is an observability company, so "agent that acts on its own traces" is the cleanest route to the 25% ceiling but also the obvious play, so that category may be crowded. The wildcard and civic ideas trade a little stack-intrinsicness for standout originality (the 10%) and a louder demo.

## The 10

1. **Mechanic** — an agent-SRE that reads another agent's neatlogs traces, diagnoses why a run failed, patches the prompt, tool schema or code, re-runs and gates on an independent verifier. Trace is the sensory organ (ceiling on the 25%), split-screen "it names the bug from the trace, re-run goes green" demo, cfo.ai prices per protected agent, pure orchestration so it ships on a t3.small. On-theme and lowest score-to-risk. Risk: low (bound the change surface, held-out verifier so it can't game the fix).

2. **Firewatch** — a self-healing on-call agent for a live service on the box. You break it on camera (kill the process, fill the disk, mispoint the ALB), it diagnoses from its traces, fixes it, then re-breaks the same fault to prove it hardened. The $25 box becomes the star, red-to-green with MTTR on screen. Risk: moderate (ship three solid fault-to-fix paths on a general hypothesis engine, not a wide shallow set).

3. **DeFlake** — hunts a real repo's flaky tests, proves the flake rate, fixes the nondeterminism, re-runs 100x to 100/100 green. Traces are the measurement, a red-wall-to-green-wall counter is the cleanest single-number demo in the set, building-in-public is native on a public repo. Risk: low (pre-scout 2-3 repos with labeled flaky tests and fast suites, keep a seeded flaky repo as fallback).

4. **Mergewright** — a real GitHub issue to a merged, canary-deployed, prod-verified change, with live auto-rollback. The money beat: the first fix passes unit tests but spikes 500s under canary traffic, the agent catches it from the canary comparison, rolls back with no user-visible breakage, then ships a corrected second attempt. Failing safely then recovering is catnip for judges scoring autonomy. Risk: moderate (pick a well-specified bug with a strong suite, canary is two ports behind the one ALB).

5. **Dial Zero** — reads your real cost stack with cfo.ai, then phones each vendor over a voice API and haggles the rate down live while the runway chart jumps. You hear an AI haggle a human and win money, the most shareable clip in the set, and cfo.ai is the brain not a bolt-on. Risk: high (real calls are brittle and can annoy real vendors, so run against your own accounts behind a confirm-before-cancel gate and keep a seeded sandbox line for the guaranteed take).

6. **Severance** — audits your SaaS and cloud bills, cancels the waste autonomously, and proves each dollar gone by re-querying the source. cfo.ai is the product (the fee is a share of realized savings), a Stripe test-mode kill is deterministic on camera with a savings counter, neatlogs is the audit log finance needs before it lets an agent cancel anything. Risk: low-moderate (headline the Stripe API path, demo portals and email as the recovery story).

7. **Crucible** — a red-team agent attacks another agent until it breaks (prompt injection, budget blowup, secret exfiltration), captures each exploit as a trace, then a hardener patches the exact hole and replays the attack to prove it bounces off. Timely security angle, exploit-lands-then-bounces is a strong demo, the trace is how a successful attack is even defined. Risk: moderate (tight sandbox with observable-but-harmless targets so nothing real escapes).

8. **First Dollar** — one line ("a paid tool that does X"), cfo.ai gates the unit economics, then the agent builds, deploys to a live public URL, wires Stripe and takes a real first payment before the video ends. A stranger's money moving on camera is an unbeatable 20%, and the economics gate the build rather than decorate it. Risk: high (browser automation across domain, deploy and Stripe is brittle, so pre-provision accounts and keys, pin one known-good deploy template, controlled test-to-live flip). Highest ceiling, highest execution risk.

9. **LedgerHound** — audits a real public-spending dataset, runs integrity tests, kills its own false positives, and publishes a receipt-backed investigation of the few flags that survive. A durable public artifact with civic impact (a real shot at the $500 community winner), Crustdata entity resolution is intrinsic (two "different" vendors sharing one owner splitting invoices to dodge a bid threshold), and the kill-your-own-false-positives arc shows restraint. Risk: low-moderate (frame every output as a flag for human review with evidence, never an accusation).

10. **Reproducer** — picks a recent CPU-feasible paper, rebuilds the environment from scratch, runs the pipeline, and files a numeric reproduced/partial/failed verdict against the paper's claim. Autonomous scientific verification is a frontier judges rarely see, the two-day cliffhanger ("can't install the deps 40 times" then "the figure matches to three decimals") is a great public arc, and Entire checkpoints the environment so a broken step restores instead of rebuilding. Risk: moderate (pre-vet a shortlist of three reproducible papers before the clock starts).

Just below the line, if you want to swap: Bisector (live git-bisect, 380 commits to 1 on screen), Scar (failures auto-compiled into a self-growing eval suite), Scrooge (AR agent negotiates a settlement then reconciles to the cent), Switchboard (change-of-address orchestrator that reads an OTP out of its own inbox). I dropped the three Crustdata sales agents (outbound is a crowded hackathon trope) and Lights-Out (needs a real API-driven 3D printer you may not have).

## My pick
Lead with **Mechanic**. It maxes the 25% because the trace is the input not the log, it genuinely ships solo in 48h on the tiny box (orchestration plus hosted LLM, no GPU), it is dead-on theme (an agent that makes agents work), and the demo is clean and repeatable. If you would rather the box be the star, **Firewatch** is the alternate. If you want the viral clip and can babysit call brittleness, **Dial Zero** is the swing.

Tell me which one and I'll scaffold the lane, pin the 48h build plan to the rubric, and line up the building-in-public cadence on X. If you want the regulated-domain lens first, say so and I'll resume that last agent.

<result>### PriorProof
- Pitch: An agent that reads a payer's medical policy and a patient's chart then assembles a submission-ready prior-authorization packet where every medical-necessity criterion is either proven against a cited passage in the record or refused and sent back as a named gap.
- The agent (30%): The task is referral plus clinical notes plus the payer's own policy PDF in, filed-ready prior-auth packet plus a criterion-by-criterion coverage matrix out. It plans by parsing the policy into an ordered list of required criteria, then runs two independent passes that must agree before any criterion turns green: one reads the policy and hunts the record for support, the other reads the record and asks which criteria it can prove, and a criterion passes only when both land on the same cited span. Any criterion the chart cannot support stays red and is never filled in by the model. Recovery: on a second pass it re-scans sections it skipped (a note filed under the wrong heading is the classic miss) and flips a red cell to green only on a real citation. Verification is the matrix itself, every green cell links to the exact page and line it rests on.
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): The coverage matrix fills in live as the neatlogs trace lights up, and the agent stops on one criterion ("failed six weeks of conservative therapy"), refuses to green it, and surfaces the empty slot with the policy line it fails against instead of inventing the note. The trust moment is an agent that will not hallucinate the one thing that gets a human denied.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs is the audit log, each policy lookup, each evidence match, each criterion decision and each refusal is a span a compliance reviewer reads to answer "why did it deny this." The agent also re-reads its own failed spans to drive the second pass. Entire checkpoints the parsed chart after extraction and the coverage state before packet assembly, so a denial that comes back weeks later branches from the coverage checkpoint rather than re-reading the whole chart, and Brain accumulates payer criteria across runs. cfo.ai models per-packet pricing against denial-reduction value and freed staff hours, with the per-run LLM API spend as a real COGS line.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): "teaching an agent to read a payer policy" on day zero, "it caught its own miss and sent the gap back" mid-build, the matrix going all-green with linked citations, then the end-to-end packet plus the audit trace. Every milestone is a screenshot of a trace, which reads as proof not marketing.
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: All inference is hosted API, the box only orchestrates, stores traces and checkpoints and serves a small demo UI, so a t3.small is plenty and the AWS spend stays trivial. Use a real public payer medical policy plus a synthetic referral and chart to avoid PHI. Biggest risk is making the eval convincing without real patient data, mitigated by one well-built synthetic case paired with a genuine published policy.
- Ambition: Prior auth is the most hated loop in US healthcare and the hard part is not drafting, it is proving each criterion and refusing to fake the one that is missing. An agent whose whole design is "prove or refuse, with the trace as evidence" is a bold claim about trustworthy automation in a regulated domain, not a summarizer.

### Redline Counsel
- Pitch: An agent that abstracts a commercial contract, measures every clause against a negotiation playbook then produces a real tracked-changes Word document plus a memo that cites each edit to the clause it fixes and the playbook rule that demanded it.
- The agent (30%): Contract from EDGAR plus a position playbook (preferred language, fallback positions and walk-aways) in, redlined DOCX plus negotiation memo out. It plans a clause inventory, extracts each clause into a structured term sheet, classifies each as acceptable, negotiate or reject, drafts the playbook's language for the ones that fail, then reconciles edits against each other so fixing a liability cap does not silently break an indemnity that references it. Recovery: when two edits conflict it walks the clause dependency graph and reorders or merges them. Verification is a round trip, it re-abstracts its own redlined document and confirms every reject and negotiate clause now meets the playbook while no acceptable clause was touched, and it rejects the run if a cited heading or clause number does not exist verbatim in the source.

An agent writing a genuine redlined DOCX, not a summary of what it would change, is the reveal.

Entire checkpoints the abstracted term sheet and playbook decisions, so you branch an aggressive stance and a moderate stance from the same checkpoint (Trails are the two negotiation lines, Graph is the clause dependency graph the reconciliation walks) and Brain carries the playbook across contracts. cfo.ai models a per-contract redline fee against lawyer hours saved plus a legal-ops seat price, with LLM spend per contract as COGS. Crustdata is a natural bonus here, enrich the counterparty's firmographics and funding to set risk posture automatically, demanding tighter caps from a small early-stage counterparty.

Shipping real tracked changes that reconcile against each other and survive a round-trip check is a hard, auditable claim in a domain where a wrong clause costs millions.

### ClearEntry
- Pitch: An agent that classifies a product under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule by walking the General Rules of Interpretation in order, computes the duty owed then produces a filing-ready customs entry line with a legal rationale citing every rule it applied.

Recovery: if a chosen heading's text does not actually describe the product, or two derivations fork, it backtracks to the GRI step where they diverged. Verification is a convergence test, an independent top-down derivation from heading text and a bottom-up derivation from product attributes must land on the same 10-digit code, the duty math is rechecked and every cited heading must exist verbatim in the loaded schedule so no code is hallucinated.

Crustdata optionally sizes the importer market for TAM in the plan.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): "taught an agent the General Rules of Interpretation" to open, "it walked GRI one through six like a licensed broker," "it caught a misclassification worth X," then "filing-ready entry with the legal rationale." The duty-number posts carry a concrete payoff.

Biggest risk is the reasoning being credible enough on edge cases, mitigated by scoping the demo to a few tariff chapters and grounding the rationale in GRI text and published rulings rather than free-form argument.
- Ambition: Customs misclassification is a real liability with penalties and back-duties, and the correct answer is a chain of legal reasoning, not a lookup. Since a Stop hook will block me until this goal is actually met, I need to work through the house rules carefully — real working code, proper AI disclosure given this is an AI-agent hackathon, a human owner on each submission, zkasuran as the default account, and a source-available license that avoids MIT for anything competition-relevant.

I also need to resolve the fan-out width question: the standing rule says never carry a width over from an earlier run, so even though "Width 8" was set for the brainstorm phase, I need to ask again for the build phase — but that tension bumps against the Stop hook's instruction not to pause and ask the user anything.

Reading the goal-hook text more carefully, "immediately start working toward it" doesn't necessarily mean "fan out this instant without asking width" — I can begin the work while still raising the width question as a required safety parameter, not as asking "what to do."

So the resolution is: start the non-fan-out groundwork right away, and surface the width question specifically when I reach the fan-out decision point, since that's a hard stop the house rules explicitly carve out as needing a human answer.

Before fanning out, I can do real solo work — researching prior-auth primary sources (payer medical policies, medical-necessity criteria, the mandatory stack of neatlogs, Entire CLI, cfo.ai, Crustdata) and settling the architecture, like whether to build the app on Next.js and Vercel per the landing page spec.

But I should check the hosting constraint — the operator wants Vercel, which differs from PriorProof's original AWS-box plan, so I need to reconcile that with whatever approved-services rules the hackathon has for things like EC2 or Lambda.

Actually AWS is just an optional credit allowance, not a requirement, so building purely on Vercel with Next.js is fine since the mandatory stack is neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai rather than AWS. Now I need to figure out what I can actually do in this environment — starting from a non-git directory and setting up the project from scratch.

Per house rules, work happens in a specific lane folder under hackathon-hq, so I'll scaffold the project there using the provided scaffold script. For deployment, Vercel likely requires interactive login via its CLI, which falls under blocked interactive-auth steps — meaning I should build everything deploy-ready and hand off exact instructions, or use a token-based deploy if one's available.

I can create a public GitHub repo and push via the gh CLI since that's within my execution authority. The mandatory stack integrations like neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai all require signups or API keys — some involve interactive steps I can't complete myself, so I'll build the integration code and hand off the signup/credential steps clearly.

Given this, I'll build the full PriorProof app including the prove-or-refuse agent engine, coverage matrix UI, neatlogs instrumentation, Entire checkpoint integration, and a cfo.ai business plan doc, plus tests, the landing page, GitHub repo and push, Vercel deploy prep, and all submission materials like the demo video script, content page, X post, and README. The truly blocked pieces — card signups, API keys, Vercel login without a token, actual posting, and video recording — I'll prepare publish-ready and hand off with precise instructions. Now I need to map out the build phases and figure out where to parallelize work.

Starting solo, I want to first check the environment: whether a Vercel token exists, gh auth status, node/npm versions, any existing scaffold, and review scaffold.sh, landing.md, and templates. My plan: do the quick solo environment recon first (checking gh/vercel/node, scaffolding the lane, reading landing.md and templates), then ask the width question at the end of this turn before fanning out into deep research and build. That way I'm not idling while waiting on an answer, and asking "how wide" doesn't violate the no-pausing-to-ask-"what to do" rule since it's a required parameter, not a decision about direction.

Then I need to think through the conversation flow—since each turn can either run tools or end with a question, I can't run recon and ask a clarifying question in the same message, so I'll need to sequence this: run recon first, review results, then ask about width before laying out the plan.

content.content: 1 # landing.md — the recipe for winning website and landing-page frontends 2 3 Read this file IN FULL before building any website or landing page, then build to it. After shipping one, 4 append what won or what failed under "Winning flavours" at the bottom. This file is the memory of what makes 5 our frontends win, so it grows every time. **Every edit to this file is followed in the same turn by 6 `~/Downloads/hackathon-hq/bin/sync-hq-kit.sh`, so `hackathon-hq-kit.zip` always carries the current recipe.** 7 8 ## Non-negotiable defaults (every site, every time) 9 10 **The whole site's architecture and presentation is the success criterion, not an afterthought.** Every page, 11 section and state is deliberately designed: coherent information architecture, a consistent visual system, 12 clear hierarchy and spacing. A site that merely works but looks plain or disorganised is a fail, not a pass. 13 Invest the most effort here. 14 15 1. **Light AND dark mode, both first-class.** Never ship dark-only or light-only. System preference sets the 16 first paint, a visible toggle overrides it, the choice persists, and there is no flash of the wrong theme. 17 2. **A category top-menu with hover submenus.** The nav classifies the site into categories; hovering (or 18 focus, or tap on touch) opens a submenu listing that category's pages or sections. Never pile everything 19 onto one long page. 20 3. **Product-first, straight to the point, catchy.** The hero says what the thing does and gives the action. 21 Short scannable sections, real product on screen. Never a wall of text, never a report ("no CIA report"). 22 4. **Top-tier craft.** Intentional type scale, generous whitespace, one accent, restrained motion, consistent 23 radius and shadow, responsive from mobile up, AA contrast in both themes, designed empty/loading/error states. 24 25 ## Light + dark mode (the mechanism, copy this) 26 27 Put this inline in `` BEFORE any stylesheet so the theme is set before first paint (no FOUC): 28 29 ```html 30 31 ``` 32 33 Define every colour as a token, swapped by `data-theme`. Never hardcode a colour in a component: 34 35 ```css 36 :root[data-theme="light"]{ --bg:#ffffff; --ink:#0b0e14; --muted:#5b6673; --panel:#f6f8fa; --edge:#e5e9f0; --acc:#2563eb; } 37 :root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg:#0b0e14; --ink:#e6edf3; --muted:#8b98a9; --panel:#141925; --edge:#232b3a; --acc:#4a9fe0; } 38 ``` 39 40 Toggle: flip `data-theme`, persist to `localStorage`, update the toggle's icon and `aria-pressed`. Test BOTH 41 modes by eye: no invisible text, logos and images legible on both, shadows tuned per mode (dark needs softer). 42 43 ## Navigation: category top-menu with hover submenus 44 45 - A sticky top bar. Left: the logo and product name. Center or right: 3 to 6 CATEGORY items. Right end: the 46 theme toggle, and any primary call to action or connect button. 47 - Each category opens a submenu on hover AND on keyboard focus AND on tap (touch has no hover, so bind click). 48 The submenu classifies that category's pages or in-page sections, ideally with a one-line description each. 49 - Accessibility: `aria-haspopup`, `aria-expanded`, `role="menu"`, focus-visible rings, Escape closes, arrow 50 keys move. Do not trap focus. Close on outside click and on route change. 51 - Structure the SITE by these categories. If everything lives on one scroll, the categories deep-link to 52 sections; better, split into real pages or routes so each category is its own space. No clumsy single pile. 53 - **Reports and developer material each get their OWN category with a submenu, cleanly organised, never 54 scattered.** A Reports category groups the metrics, the methodology or how it is computed, the validation 55 data and the honesty or limits note. A Developers category groups the SDK, the API, the contract, the skill 56 and the docs. Decide the category taxonomy and each submenu's items deliberately BEFORE writing components. 57 Information architecture and presentation are a primary deliverable, not a wrapper around content. 58 59 ## Product-first content 60 61 - **Hero:** one line that says what the product does, plus the primary action as a button. Not a slogan, not a 62 mission statement, not three paragraphs. A subhead of one sentence is allowed. Show the product beside it 63 (a live widget, a real screenshot, a short loop), never a stock illustration. 64 - **Sections:** each is a heading, one sentence, and a visual or a real number. Bold the single number that 65 matters. A visitor scanning in ten seconds should understand the product and see proof. 66 - **Voice:** catchy and concrete, house outward-words style (no em dashes, no comma before "and" or "or", no 67 marketing fluff, no filler). Say what it does and why it is better, then stop. 68 - **Anti-pattern to avoid:** the "report" layout, a dense top-to-bottom essay with tables and no action. If it 69 reads like a dossier, rebuild it as a product page. 70 71 ## Craft that reads as top-tier 72 73 - One type family, a real scale (for example 12 / 14 / 16 / 20 / 28 / 40), line-height ~1.5 for body. 74 - Generous, consistent spacing on an 8px rhythm. One accent colour used sparingly for action and emphasis. 75 - Motion is restrained: hover and reveal transitions around 150 to 250ms, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`, 76 no gratuitous parallax or autoplay. 77 - Consistent corner radius and a shadow system tuned per theme. Real or representative data, with designed 78 empty, loading and error states. For ANY chart, gauge or KPI tile, invoke the `dataviz` skill first. 79 80 ## Spacing and layout rhythm 81 82 Spacing is not filler, it is what makes a site read as calm and premium. Get it wrong and even great content 83 looks broken. 84 85 - Vertical rhythm on an 8px scale, EVEN and BALANCED. Sections get consistent, COMPACT padding (roughly 40 to 86 56px top and bottom on desktop, less on mobile), the same on every section. Equal spacing everywhere, no 87 section stretched and no section crammed. The aim is a cohesive page, not a long wall of air. 88 - **A sticky or fixed header must never overlap content.** The header needs a fully opaque or backdrop-blurred 89 background so content scrolling beneath it never bleeds through the nav. Set `scroll-padding-top` on the 90 scroll root (html) and `scroll-margin-top` on every deep-linkable section equal to the header height plus a 91 small gap, so anchor and submenu navigation lands BELOW the header, not tucked under it. The first section 92 starts below the header, not beneath it. 93 - Constrain and center content in a max-width container (about 1100 to 1280px) with consistent left and right 94 gutters. Full-bleed body text is hard to read. 95 - Remove empty space, do not just add it. Size charts, panels and media to their content so there are no large 96 dead areas (a chart with a few bars does not need 300px of height). Use two-column or grid layouts to fill 97 horizontal space rather than stacking everything into one tall column. Keep gaps inside cards and grids 98 consistent (12 / 16 / 24). When a region looks empty, tighten or fill it, never paper over it with more padding. 99 - Test WHILE SCROLLING and at real widths (360, 768, 1280, 1920), not just at the top, to catch header overlap 100 and cramped sections. 101 102 ## Hardening (every site, as standard as the dark mode) 103 104 A winning site is also one a reviewer cannot break from the browser console. Reference: `work/hailjury/web`. 105 106 - **Strict CSP, generated at build time.** A Vite (or equivalent) plugin injects 107 `` only into the production build (dev needs inline HMR): 108 `default-src 'none'`, `script-src 'self'` plus the sha256 hash of the no-FOUC theme script (plus 109 `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` if you ship WebAssembly), `connect-src 'self'` plus the exact API hosts, 110 `img-src 'self' data:`, `font-src 'self' data:` (bundlers inline small fonts), `base-uri 'none'`, 111 `form-action 'none'`, `object-src 'none'`. Then load the built site and confirm zero CSP violations 112 in the console. 113 - **Response headers for the host.** A `public/_headers` with `frame-ancestors 'none'` (meta CSP cannot set 114 it), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, HSTS and a deny-all 115 `Permissions-Policy`. 116 - **Escape anything rendered as HTML.** Any `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (syntax-highlighted JSON, code) escapes 117 `&`, `<` and `>` first. Prefer text nodes everywhere else. 118 - **An error boundary around the routed view**, keyed on the route so it resets on navigation. One broken 119 page must never blank the header, the menu or the rest of the site. 120 - **Every fetch has a timeout and a validated shape.** `AbortController` at a few seconds, a size cap, 121 shape checks before use. If the answer is signed, verify it, and confirm it answers the question asked. 122 - **Browser storage is user-editable.** Wrap every `JSON.parse` of `localStorage`, validate the shape, 123 re-verify signatures, cap list lengths and survive quota errors. Our own static JSON fixtures are 124 re-verified before render too. 125 - **Validate route params** (ids, slugs) against a strict pattern before fetching anything with them. 126 - **Designed failure states:** loading skeletons, an offline or relay-down state, an engine-failed state. 127 These are tested by forcing them (bad slug, tampered storage, no network), not assumed. 128 129 ## The GitHub README (a landing page that lives in the repo) 130 131 Same rules as a site: product first, scannable, real product on screen, nothing a reader has to trust. 132 GitHub strips scripts and most CSS, so the craft is in the assets and the structure. 133 134 - **Themes:** wrap every visual in ` 135 `, so the banner and screenshots match the reader's GitHub theme. 136 - **Banner:** a 1280 x 400 hand-made SVG per theme. Use system font stacks (GitHub renders SVG through 137 ``, so web fonts never load) and keep text inside the safe left 60%. Render it with 138 `google-chrome --headless=new --screenshot` and look at it before committing. 139 - **Screenshots:** captured from the live deploy with Playwright at `deviceScaleFactor: 2` and 140 `colorScheme` set per theme. Scroll through the page first so scroll-reveal sections render, and wait 141 for animations to settle (assert on computed opacity, not just presence). A screenshot caught 142 mid-animation reads as a broken product. 143 - **Diagrams:** Mermaid fenced blocks (`sequenceDiagram`, `flowchart LR`). Label edges with what moves. 144 - **Tables over prose:** try-it steps, use cases, trust model, checks, real versus simulated. 145 - **Badges:** static shields.io stating proven facts. Never a status badge that 404s for anonymous 146 viewers of a private repo. 147 - **Anchors:** the nav row links to `#section-slugs`. Check that every one resolves on github.com. 148 149 ## Pre-ship checklist 150 151 - [ ] Light and dark both look intentional, the toggle persists, no flash of the wrong theme (head script present). 152 - [ ] Category top-menu with submenus that open on hover, on keyboard focus, and on tap. 153 - [ ] Site is split by category, not one clumsy pile on a single page. 154 - [ ] Hero states what the product does in one line with a primary action button; the product is shown, not described. 155 - [ ] Sections are scannable with the key number bolded; no report or wall-of-text layout. 156 - [ ] Responsive from mobile to desktop, keyboard accessible, AA contrast in both themes. 157 - [ ] No sticky-header overlap: content clears the header on load and on anchor navigation, the header 158 background is opaque, sections have consistent generous spacing (checked while scrolling, not just at the top). 159 - [ ] Real or representative data, with empty, loading and error states designed. 160 - [ ] Every chart or gauge went through the `dataviz` skill. 161 - [ ] All copy is in house outward-words style (no em dashes, no comma before "and" or "or", no filler). 162 - [ ] Production build carries a strict CSP; loaded in headless Chrome with zero console errors and zero CSP violations. 163 - [ ] `_headers` present; error boundary around routes; every fetch has a timeout; storage and route params validated. 164 - [ ] Failure paths forced and screenshotted: bad id, tampered storage, network down, engine failed to load. 165 - [ ] Repo README follows "The GitHub README": themed banner and screenshots, Mermaid diagrams, try-it table, real vs simulated table, all links and images checked anonymously. 166 - [ ] Gated by the repo's `verify.sh` (typecheck, tests, build, `npm audit` at 0) and run by CI. 167 168 ## Winning flavours (lessons, newest first) 169 170 * 2026-10-03 — Never drive read-along highlighting from the Web Speech API. On Linux Chrome it is a 171 scratchy espeak voice, `onboundary` fires late or not at all, and pause then resume restarts the 172 utterance from the top while the highlight stays put. Pre-render narration with a TTS that returns 173 word timestamps (Kokoro-82M does, Apache-2.0, CPU is fine) and drive everything from ONE clock: the 174 audio element's `currentTime` when voice is on, a virtual clock otherwise. Pause, seek, voice toggle 175 and chapter change then only ever write that number, and a headless test can assert the lit word 176 matches `currentTime` in every scenario. A looping float animation on the player also made the voice 177 button "not stable" for Playwright clicks; real users notice that too. 178 179 * 2026-10-03 — A site that ships a browser port of a backend rule (a guardrail, a tuner) earns trust only 180 if a test holds the two together. Nightjar exports the Python verdicts and predictions as fixtures and a 181 node test demands the TypeScript port match them byte for byte and to 1e-6; the playground then shows 182 "Python agrees" live. Separately, an in-browser model can work in your dev browser and fail in a 183 visitor's: onnxruntime-web's asyncify build has no CPU kernel for `GatherBlockQuantized`, so the 184 quantised Gemma loaded fine with WebGPU and threw on every machine without it. Run the lab once in 185 headless Chrome with no GPU before calling it done, and pick the plain ORT build for the CPU path. 186 187 * 2026-10-01 — Taking README screenshots is a free QA pass. Hail Jury's Audit tab looked half-empty in 188 every capture because a countdown re-rendered the room every 250 ms, and the view rebuilt its bundle 189 object each time, so the audit re-ran and restarted its animation forever. Users would have seen a 190 verdict that never fully faded in. `useMemo` on the derived object fixed it.
