## Licensing (strict, and enforced by the build not by memory)

Learned the expensive way on Telegraph: we published competition binaries under MIT,
and MIT is precisely the permission to take a registered artifact, append a few bytes
that rescale its output, and register the result as a rival entry. Twelve scorer slots
were taken from us that way, every one decoding to our own base plus a two-band map,
and every one of those takings was lawful. A miner deployment (`livecert`) was found
running our answer templates too. None of that is a complaint about anyone's conduct;
it is a correction of our own licence choice, and these rules exist so the choice is
never made carelessly again.

### 1. Default outbound licence: source-available, no derivatives

Anything we publish that competes on a public leaderboard, or that a rival can fetch
and re-register, ships under **Source-Available No-Derivatives** (SPDX
`LicenseRef-zkasuran-SAND-1.0`), not MIT. The reference text is
`work/telegraph/scorer/LICENSE`; copy it, do not re-draft it.

It grants what a reader, validator or judge needs and nothing more: run it for any
purpose including commercially, read it, decompile it, benchmark it, publish what you
find. It withholds exactly one thing, redistribution and derivative works, because
that is the thing that was used against us.

MIT (or Apache-2.0 where a program demands a patent grant) is correct for a genuine
upstream contribution: a PR into someone else's repo takes that repo's licence, and a
standalone library meant to be adopted wants adoption. The test is whether the artifact
is a **contribution** or an **entry**. Contributions get permissive terms. Entries get
SAND.

### 2. The licence goes in the bytes

A binary fetched from a raw URL arrives with no `LICENSE`, no `NOTICE` and no README, so
terms that live only in a repository are terms the holder never sees. Put them inside
the artifact:

- wasm: an inert custom section (`work/telegraph/scorer/rev/stamp.py`). The runtime
  ignores custom sections, so behaviour and exports are unchanged and `strings x.wasm`
  shows the terms.
- other binaries: an equivalent inert region, or a sidecar the fetch instructions name.
- source, JSON descriptors, YAML: an SPDX header line.

Make the pipeline refuse, rather than trusting anyone to remember. `reg_batch.py` will
not register an unstamped file without an explicit `--allow-unstamped`, and that is the
pattern to copy: **the publish step verifies the licence, or the publish step is wrong.**

### 3. Upstream first when the artifact is mostly someone else's

When a build's bulk is another author's work reused under their licence, their terms
govern those portions and ours cover only our addition. Say so **before** our own
notice, in the bytes, so a reader who only runs `strings` still lands on the right
licence. `stamp.py --upstream URL --upstream-licence SPDX --upstream-copyright LINE`
does this, and it refuses a URL given without both the licence and the copyright line:
naming a source without its terms is worse than not naming it.

### 4. Lineage is read off the bytes, never hand-maintained

`PROVENANCE.json` is generated (`rev/provenance.py`) by fingerprinting every published
file and grouping each build with its base, so the record cannot drift from what is
actually published. Three states, and only three:

| lineage | meaning | licence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `own` | our source, our build | SAND-1.0 |
| `source_fork` | built from another author's **source** under a licence permitting it | theirs, named, plus ours on our addition |
| `binary_wrap` | another author's **compiled binary** plus our bytes | not publishable |

`binary_wrap` must read zero. If one appears, the file is withdrawn, recorded in
`WITHDRAWN.json` with the reason, and it stays withdrawn even when it would win. We
withdrew 44 such files on 2026-08-30 and that decision is not reopened because a slot
is close.

### 5. Every third-party input needs a quotable clause

Before any data source, model weight, font, image or audio track enters a build, read
its terms and record the exact granting sentence in the lane's `DATA-SOURCES.md`. If
the grant cannot be quoted the source does not ship, and the answer says what is
missing rather than serving something we may not republish.

Two verdicts from the Telegraph audit worth carrying forward, because they are the
shapes that catch people out:

- "Free API" is not a licence. Open-Meteo's free tier is non-commercial only, so it
  came out of every miner and was replaced with MET Norway (CC BY 4.0 + NLOD 2.0) and
  the US NWS ("free to use for any purpose"). A rival still running open-meteo is on
  the wrong side of a clause we already moved off.
- No stated licence at all means no permission to redistribute a modified copy. Absence
  of terms is not permission.

Attribution that a licence requires is not optional and is not "framing": CC BY, ODbL
and MIT all require it, and the credit goes where a user of the artifact sees it.

### 6. Licence changes are dated, bounded and irrevocable backwards

A licence change never claws anything back. Record the boundary commit, state which
grant covers which period, and say plainly that anyone who obtained a copy under the
old terms keeps them and owes nothing.
`work/telegraph/scorer/LICENSE-HISTORY.md` is the template.

### 7. Before any repo flips public

Check, in this order: `LICENSE` present and correct for entry-vs-contribution;
`NOTICE` naming every third-party component with its own terms; `PROVENANCE.json`
regenerated with `binary_wrap: 0`; every published binary carrying its section
(`stamp.py --check` returns clean); `DATA-SOURCES.md` quoting a clause per source;
and no private-data file (`submit/`, form fills, keys) tracked. A public repo is a
publication, and a publication with the wrong licence cannot be un-published.

## Storage management (measure, repack, then delete, in that order)

Learned on 2026-09-03, when the 483G root hit 95% full with 25G left. A 23-area audit
reclaimed 222G. The single biggest win was not a deletion. This section is the whole rule.
It complements **Reuse before rebuilding** in step 2 of the method: that one says do not pay
for an install twice, this one says do not keep what nobody will read again.

### Trigger and order

Above 85% on `/`, reclaim. Below that, leave it alone and spend the turns on lanes.

Always in this order, cheapest and most reversible first: measure, repack, delete. Start with
`df -h /` and `du -xm --max-depth=5 /home/asuran | sort -rn | head -40`. Get the whole
inventory before touching anything. A reclaim that starts with an `rm` is a reclaim that
deletes the wrong thing.

### Repack before deleting anything

Run `git count-objects -v` on every repo over a few hundred MB. A large `size:` with
`in-pack: 0` means loose objects, which get zlib but no delta compression, so every
historical version of every blob is stored whole.

`work/telegraph/scorer` held 3363 loose objects at 15,681 MB because `dist/` is tracked and
holds ~1769 near-identical 29 MB wasm blobs. A plain `git gc` took `.git` to 1,076 MB. That
is 14.6G freed with nothing deleted, nothing to re-download, on a repo carrying 257 dirty
files that no `rm` is allowed near. `scorer-lab` had the same disease at smaller scale.

Use plain `git gc`, not `--prune=now`, so the default two-week window keeps recent
unreachable objects. Sweep for this before proposing a single deletion.

### What makes a tree disposable

All four, not three: an origin remote, a clean `git status --porcelain`, an empty
`git log --branches --not --remotes`, an empty `git stash list`. Miss one and the tree holds
work that exists nowhere else.

Stale remote-tracking refs overstate the unpushed count. teleworld reported 176 of 198
worktrees carrying unique work and the true answer was none, because those counts came from
refs that had never been fetched. Confirm against the live remote before believing a big
number. See [[teleworld-local-state-is-disposable]].

Worktree branches live in the main repo's `.git`, provable with
`git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, so `git worktree remove` destroys only uncommitted content
and never a commit. Commit the dirty ones first, then remove the directories with
`git worktree remove --force` so the metadata goes too.

### Extract, then delete

When a large tree is kept only for a small amount of unique work, take the work out rather
than keeping the tree.

- Tracked changes: commit them on their own branch, then `git format-patch -1` into the lane.
  The patch carries its parent SHA, so `git am` refuses on a wrong base instead of misapplying.
- Untracked files: copy them to the lane root, beside the results they produced.
- Write a `RESTORE-*.md` naming the clone URL, the base SHA, the apply step plus any
  submodule init the build needs.
- Verify with `git apply --check --reverse` before the `rm`. Gate the `rm` on the saved file
  existing and being non-empty.

On 2026-09-03 `3mdeb-lane/902/coreboot` (1,881 MB) and `tenstorrent/build/tt-metal` (719 MB)
were held by 69 and 124 lines respectively. Both trees went, both changes survive as a patch
and a file.

### Never delete

- Everything protected by **Licensing** and the FLOP spec: `../flop/work/flop/identity/`, any key,
  `.passphrase` or `.env*`, any `submit/`, any `DEMO-*.mp4` or `upload-*/`, packets and state
  docs, `PROVENANCE.json` with the bytes it fingerprints.
- Any repo with no origin remote. `work/bond` is the standing example and gets its
  `node_modules` taken and nothing else. See [[bond-lane-has-no-remote]].
- `~/.config/google-chrome`. It holds the live login cookies that headless work copies.
- A live lane's inputs. A dataset counts as regenerable only when the exact download command
  can be named. If it cannot be named, it is irreplaceable whatever its size, which is why
  `work/virtual-embryo/external/jax` keeps 10.1G.
- A model cache that a script opens with `local_files_only=True`. Deleting that is a hard
  failure, not a silent re-download.

### Measure honestly

Hardlink farms double count: `.cache/uv` into every venv, `.cargo/git/db` into `checkouts`,
mamba `pkgs` into `envs`. Run `du -csm` over the pair for the real gain.

Trust the `df` delta, never the sum of per-path `du`. The 2026-09-03 per-path sum predicted
202G where the real figure was 185G.

Some trees resist `rm` inside home. `go/pkg/mod` needs `go clean -modcache`. NuGet caches
plus waydroid data are root-owned. sudo has no password in session, so `/var` work (journal,
snapd, logs, swapfile) is a handoff with exact commands, not a blocked step.

### Leave a record

Write the vetted paths to `work/RECLAIM-<date>.txt` before running them, then keep the file.

Once a lane's deadline has passed and its outcome is recorded in the tracker, its build
artifacts are fair game. Clearing them then is cheaper than an emergency sweep at 95%. The
full account of what was freed, what stays and why is in [[reclaim-disk-space-audit]].

## MiniMax (Max plan, through ~2026-12-18) — default AI provider for submission builds

For the next 3 months every submission build that needs an LLM, text-to-speech or reasoning uses the
MiniMax Max plan by default. OpenAI-compatible, one Bearer key. This supplements the house LLM gateway
rule for submission-building work; where a program forbids a given provider, follow the program.

* **Base URL:** `https://api.minimax.io/v1` (mirror `https://api.minimaxi.chat/v1`). Auth header
  `Authorization: Bearer $MINIMAX_API_KEY`.
* **Key:** `MINIMAX_API_KEY` in `~/Downloads/hackathon-hq/.minimax.env`, mode 600. Never in a repo,
  never printed, never pasted into a PR, issue, form or chat. Source at point of use:
  `set -a && . ~/Downloads/hackathon-hq/.minimax.env && set +a`.
* **Text / reasoning:** `MiniMax-M3` (flagship, reasoning — emits `<think>...</think>` then the answer),
  plus `MiniMax-M2.7 / M2.5 / M2.1` and their `-highspeed` variants for cheaper, faster calls. Chat via
  OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` or native `/v1/text/chatcompletion_v2`.
* **Voice (TTS):** `POST /v1/t2a_v2`, model `speech-02-hd` (or `speech-01`). No GroupId needed on this
  key. Returns `data.audio` as a HEX string of an mp3 (decode hex to bytes). Use for demo-video narration.
* **Music:** NOT on this key (410, "no longer available to new users"). Keep using the house
  no-copyright track for videos.
* Verified 2026-09-18: /v1/models, chat, and t2a all 200; music 410.

## Tooling

Lane-specific rules live in that lane's own `CLAUDE.md` and override the general habits
here where they conflict. `work/virtual-embryo/CLAUDE.md` is the live example: on a scored
leaderboard the goal is rank, so only point-scale jumps count and a confirmed knob gets
swept at x2 to x3 spacing until the board turns over before anything new is built.

- `gh auth status` (zkasuran should be active)
- `gh pr view <N> --repo <repo> --comments`
- `gh pr checks <N> --repo <repo>`
- `gh pr create --repo <upstream> --base main --head zkasuran:<branch> --title ... --body-file ...`
- Post a comment or set a PR body from a file with `-F body=@<file>`, never `-f`.
  `-f` sends the string literally, so `-f body=@reply.md` posts the text `@reply.md`
  and you have to delete the comment and repost. `gh pr edit --body` is a silent
  no-op on these repos, so PATCH a body over REST:
  `gh api -X PATCH repos/<O>/<R>/pulls/<n> -F body=@<file>` and verify the live body.
  See memory `gh-pr-edit-body-fails-use-rest`.
- Run the project's own commands: `pytest`, `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`,
  `mypy`, or whatever the repo uses. Match the repo, not a default.

### Looking at images: never read anything over 2000 px

The image reader refuses any image whose longest edge is over 2000 px once a conversation already
holds many images. The refusal is not a skipped picture: it fails the whole turn and the work stops.
Screenshots taken at `deviceScaleFactor: 2` come out 2100 to 2500 px wide, so they trip it every time.
On 2026-10-05 a README art check died mid-task this way.

- **Never pass an original screenshot to the reader.** Make a review copy first and read that:
  `python3 bin/preview-image.py <file.png> [more.png ...]`. It writes `/tmp/preview/<dir>-<name>.png`
  with the longest edge at most 1800 px and prints the path. `--max` lowers it further.
- **SVG is not readable as an image at all.** Render it to PNG first with a headless Chrome
  screenshot at its own size (1280 wide for the README art), then preview that.
- **Read at most four images per call.** Preview only the ones that answer the question. Every
  image read stays in the conversation and counts toward the many-image limit.
- **Keep shipping files at 2x.** The limit applies to what is read for review, never to what is
  published. Downscale the copy, not the asset.

## Disclosure template (adapt per PR)

> AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) was used in developing this change. The
> design, review and verification were done by the author. Verified locally
> before submitting: <the tests/lint/type-checks that pass>.

Keep prose clean and specific. Lead with the author's ownership. The AI line is
a brief factual note, not the headline. Do not overclaim what the human reviewed;
state what was actually verified.

## Writing style (PR text, comments, docs, commit messages)

Write like a human, not an AI. This is about voice only. It does not change
principle 2: the AI disclosure stays. Clean human prose plus an honest
disclosure is the goal, not hiding that AI helped.

Write it clean from the first token. These rules are a drafting habit, not a
cleanup pass. Hold them in mind as the text is written rather than emitting AI
prose and scrubbing it after: the scrub wastes turns (each is $0.10) and a slip
that reaches a reviewer costs a whole round. Every subagent brief that produces
outward words puts these rules at the top, framed as "do not emit these", not
"fix these later".

- No em dashes. Use a comma, a period, parentheses or a rewrite instead.
- No comma before "and" or "or". No Oxford comma, and no comma-before-and habit.
- No AI tells or filler. Drop "it's worth noting", "in conclusion", "delve",
  "robust", "seamless", "leverage", forced three-item lists, throat-clearing
  and hedging.
- Short direct sentences. Plain words. Vary the length so it reads natural.
- Say what changed and why. Skip the marketing voice.

Applies to every outward word: PR titles and bodies, issue and review comments,
commit messages and docs.

**The gate is a command now, not a habit.** `bin/voice-gate.mjs` checks em dashes,
comma-before-and and the AI tells above, and `bin/portal-post.sh` runs it before any
request leaves the machine and refuses to POST on a hit. Use `portal-post.sh` for
dashboard updates and mentor replies rather than hand-rolling curl.

    node bin/voice-gate.mjs body.txt
    PORTAL_SESSION=... bin/portal-post.sh reply <question-id> body.txt

This exists because on 2026-09-25 I posted an update and four mentor replies without
running the grep: 15 em dashes and 18 comma-before-and went out. The update was
revisable. **The mentor replies were not.** `PATCH` and `PUT` on a reply both return
404, so no edit route exists, and an answered question returns 409
`INVALID_STATE_TRANSITION`. Those four replies are permanent. Deliberate exceptions
take `voice-gate:allow` on the line, or a `voice-gate:off` / `voice-gate:on` fence for
quoted text such as verbatim licence wording.

One pre-send gate, because these models drift back to em dashes and Oxford commas
in long output no matter the instruction. A #42 comment once went out with 14
comma-before-and slips despite the rule. Before posting anything outward, grep the
text for em dashes and for `, and` / `, or` and fix any hit. Treat it like a linter
over code you already meant to write clean: an empty result is the expected state,
not a surprise, and it is not the mechanism, the clean drafting is. Upstream
template wording quoted inside our PR body (the checklist lines) is theirs, leave
those commas alone.

## Frame the work as our own

Our designs, docs and outputs present our own ideas in our own voice. They are
not a literature review of who we borrowed from, and not a derivative of prior
work dressed up with citations. State the idea plainly as ours.

Do not scatter inline references through the body: no file-and-line pointers to
our own prior builds, no "adapted from", "lifted from" or "ported from", no
naming another platform as the source of a design choice. Our prior work is ours
already, so it needs no citation. Experience is a strength to state, not a
reference to attach.

Give explicit credit only where something demands it. A source license that
requires attribution gets it. A platform or program that requires disclosure gets
it, and the AI disclosure in principle 2 is exactly that kind of demand and it
stays. Absent a demand, our voice and our design.

This is framing, not dishonesty. The honesty floor does not move: never state an
external fact we have not verified as settled (a contract address, an ABI, a
third-party parameter), and never claim a human reviewed what no human read.
Internal tracking notes, a lane ledger or a reuse comment we keep for our own
benefit, are not outward credit and are fine.

## Resume

On "continue" or a new session: read `START-HERE.md`, check live PR status, then open
Hackathon HQ for the full reminder feed: `node work/hq/hq.mjs remind` for the digest or
`node work/hq/hq.mjs serve` for the dashboard on http://127.0.0.1:7788. HQ is the
consolidated view over deadlines, winner-announcement checks, PRs and bounties in one
place, sharing the same store as the opportunity tracker (`node work/opps/opps.mjs due`
is the narrower deadline-and-recheck slice of it). HQ records each project's
lifecycle phase on its own through SessionStart and Stop hooks that run `hq scan`,
so progress from building through finished, submitted, deadline passed and winner
day writes itself down with nothing to hand-maintain. Respond to any maintainer activity,
then pick the next target and triage it live (dedupe first with
`node work/opps/opps.mjs check`, record the verdict with `opps add` or `opps set`; set a
lane's outcome once results land with `node work/hq/hq.mjs results`).
Operate under **Execution authority** and **Content cadence** above for every
target, the same way, from the first action of the session. On anything touching
flop-labs, technocore.chat or $FLOP, `../flop/CLAUDE.md` applies from the first
commit, not at submit time.

Contents of /home/asuran/Downloads/hackathon-hq/CLAUDE.md:

# Hackathon HQ: the playbook

Goal: win hackathon bounties by landing genuine, high-quality, merged
contributions. We compete on craft, not volume.

## Principles (non-negotiable)

1. **Real work only.** Every submission is a genuine fix, feature, or example the
   project actually wants, with tests that pass. If it would not stand on its own
   as a useful contribution, we do not send it.
2. **AI disclosed wherever the program requires it.** unitaryHACK and most bounty
   programs require it, and for those we disclose every time: hiding it means
   disqualification and a ban ("honesty is a requirement for bounty eligibility").
   Put the disclosure where the program actually reads it (the PR body) and state
   what AI did and what was verified. Don't pad beyond that: once the PR body
   discloses, no need to repeat it in commit trailers. Where a program genuinely
   has no disclosure requirement, follow that program's rules. Never present
   AI-written work as undisclosed where disclosure is expected.
3. **A human owns each PR.** The person behind the account must understand the
   change well enough to explain it in a live conversation and answer maintainer
   questions. AI does most of the typing; the human reviews, submits, and defends.
   Never claim a human reviewed code that no human read.
4. **Accounts are the operator's call.** `zkasuran` is the main identity and the
   default when nothing says otherwise. Other GitHub identities are live in the gh
   keyring and more get added over time, so never assume a fixed roster or count:
   read it live with `gh auth status` and switch with `gh auth switch --user <name>`.
   How many accounts to enter a given program with is decided per program by
   zkasuran, not by a rule in this file. Two things still bind: a program's own
   eligibility rules where it limits entries per person, and principle 3 — the
   submitting account owns the work and must be able to defend it. Record which
   account each submission went out under in `participations.md`.
5. **Green before submit.** Clone, understand, change, then run the project's own
   tests + lint + type-check. All green, or it is not done.
6. **In the FLOP ecosystem, the DID is attached.** Anything for flop-labs,
   technocore.chat or $FLOP ships with our `did:key`, a signature over the
   published bytes plus a signed post on the service. The spec is `../flop/CLAUDE.md`.
   Unsigned work there is work that cannot be credited to us.
7. **Strict licensing, in the bytes, before anything ships.** Every artifact we
   publish carries its own terms and its own lineage, and every third-party input
   is used only under a clause we have read and can quote. Default outbound licence
   is source-available no-derivatives, never MIT, for anything that competes.
   See **Licensing** below. An unlicensed or unattributed artifact does not ship.

## What we do NOT do

- No undisclosed AI.
- No low-effort or duplicate PRs. No deleting failing tests to "pass" CI. No
  hallucinated or nonexistent APIs.
- No claiming human review that did not happen.
- No unsigned FLOP-ecosystem artifact, and never a second `did:key`. One identity,
  attached, or the work does not ship.
- No artifact published without its licence in its own bytes, no derivative of
  someone else's work without their terms named first, and no third-party data
  source whose grant we have not read. See **Licensing**.

## The method (per target)

1. **Triage live.** Is the issue open and unclaimed? Is there already a rival PR
   solving it? Is the toolchain buildable here (native deps, sudo, interpreter
   version)? Verify against the live repo before investing. Triage labels and
   notes go stale fast. For DoraHacks targets, run the standard roster->detail
   rival scan and decode the rubric every time (the how-to + reusable script
   `work/dorahacks-research.mjs` are in memory `dorahacks-research-method`), and
   re-run it right before submitting (`pre-submit-rival-pr-check`).
2. **Set up.** Clone into the build workspace. Build the toolchain / venv. Get the
   existing test suite green as a baseline before touching anything.
   **Reuse before rebuilding (saves AI credits and wall clock).** Before any
   fresh clone, install or research pass, check whether a sibling lane already
   paid that cost and copy it instead:
   - Same repo, another issue already built here: copy `node_modules`/venv/
     `target` from the sibling clone (e.g. `cp -a ../<sibling>/node_modules .`
     then one fix-up install), reuse its baseline test counts as the expected
     baseline, and reuse its learned repo facts (default branch, flaky
     registry, required check order) instead of rediscovering them.
   - Same repo conventions already studied (adapter blueprint, test style,
     receipt format): point the new build at the sibling packet/PR rather
     than re-reading the whole repo cold.
   - Cross-repo knowledge counts too: if we built or deeply studied a
     protocol in one lane (its SDK, addresses, call shapes), lift that into
     any lane that touches the same protocol, with attribution in a comment.
     Never blind-copy diffs between different issues; reuse the paid-for
     context, write the change fresh for the issue at hand.
   Record durable repo facts (default branch, install quirks, baseline
   counts) in the lane ledger so the next lane starts warm.
3. **Read the real code.** Map the exact change surface. Verify against source;
   do not trust summaries or memory.
4. **Research first, before writing code.** Whenever the change leans on a paper,
   spec, standard, formula or external API, read the primary source FIRST and let
   it shape the design, not the other way round. Do this BEFORE implementing, not
   as a polish pass at the end. We learned this the hard way on mitiq #2936: the
   research ran last and caught a real citation error (the canonical-scaling math
   was Mari_2021_PRA, not Kim_2023_Nature) that had been baked through the
   docstring, the docs and the first PR body. Done first, it would never have been
   wrong. Concretely: pull the actual paper/section the issue cites (web search +
   read it), verify the math or behavior against it, and pin every citation to the
   repo's own bibliography key (grep the .bib) rather than a bare URL. A quick web
   pass for newer work is fine, but stay on scope: cite what the change uses, do
   not bolt on a literature review.

   **A program's own resources library and mentor roster are primary sources, not
   background reading.** Where a hackathon ships them, mine them BEFORE designing
   any module, in this order: the dependency's own **source repo** (docs lag, types
   do not), then **official docs including the host's**, then the **portal
   resources**, then **a mentor for what only a human can settle**. Never ask a
   human what step one to three answers.
   > On Monad Metropolis, reading a weeks-old SDK's source found two facts that broke
   > our design before a line was written: deriving N key namespaces cost N user
   > prompts, which contradicted a bounty's own one-prompt deliverable, and one common
   > browser-plus-extension combination returns no key material at all, which would
   > have surfaced during the live judged gate. Neither is in training data. Separately
   > the host's own guide called a registry "coming soon" while it was live on mainnet.

   **Mentor and support channels are async, so ask one phase ahead of the build,
   never when blocked.** Write the ask-by date against the phase that needs the
   answer. Log every question and its answer in the lane ledger with the date: an
   organizer-reviewed answer is the closest thing to a ruling a program gives you,
   and it outranks your own reasoning about the same question.

   **Mechanics are safe to ask in public, intent is not.** How an API behaves tells
   rivals nothing. What you want it for can hand over the whole thesis. The same line
   applies to a public forum and a reviewed mentor channel.
5. **Implement.** Make the real change, matching repo conventions and comment
   style. Test-driven where it fits. Keep the diff focused. **Follow the target's
   explicit asks.** When the issue or a maintainer names a concrete file, API,
   structure or approach, default to it. That is the path they merge and the path a
   rival who follows it looks aligned with. Deviate only with a concrete reason it
   is worse. When you do, weigh both paths against their stated preference and the
   rubric, choose deliberately and record the why in the packet so it can be
   defended. Offer to match their structure if they ask. Cleaner is never the goal
   on its own. Merged is.
6. **Verify.** Run tests + lint + type-check. Capture the real output. If anything
   fails or is skipped, say so. Never report green that is not.
7. **Write a submit packet.** Plain-English walkthrough (so the human can explain
   it as if in a live interview), a ready PR body filling the repo's template,
   the AI disclosure, and the likely maintainer Q&A.
8. **Human submits + engages.** The human reviews, opens the PR, and answers the
   maintainer. After merge, follow the program's bounty-claim step.
9. **In the FLOP ecosystem, attach the DID before step 8.** Sign the artifact,
   publish the note, leave the signed post, cite the `seq`. See `../flop/CLAUDE.md`.
   A FLOP contribution submitted without this is incomplete, not merely unpolished.

## Devpost submissions: drive the whole thing headless, the human only clicks Create project

Devpost's submission manager is plain Rails forms, so once a draft exists the entry is
filled AND submitted headlessly from a logged-in browser cURL. Only one step is gated: the
invisible reCAPTCHA on the Create project button. Everything else is written over the API:
title, tagline, description, tags, the try-it link, the video URL, the submitter and
eligibility fields, the sponsor questions, the thumbnail image and the final submit. The
final Submit is NOT a captcha wall, it is just a terms checkbox
(`participants_manage_finalization[accepts_terms]=1`) posted to the `finalization` form, so
we submit it too. Submitting before the deadline is reversible on Devpost (edit or
withdraw). The entries point to human-owned, human-defended work, so submitting is
within **Execution authority**, not a hand-off.

Do not build a click-to-copy field-by-field HTML page for a Devpost entry. That is the
right shape for a form we cannot drive (see **Content cadence**). Devpost is not one.
The workflow for any Devpost hackathon is:

1. Ask the human to press Create project once per entry, then to hand over the browser
   cURL for the manager (DevTools "copy as cURL" on any `manage/submissions` page). Save
   its cookie at the workspace root as `.devpost.cookie`, mode 0600, never inside a clone.
   The load-bearing values are `_devpost`, `remember_user_token`, `jwt` and `aws-waf-token`,
   and the session goes stale in about a day, so a fresh cURL is the routine ask, not a
   failure.
2. Claim whatever empty drafts exist, map each to a project and fill every field for
   every draft headlessly, thumbnail included. Verify by reading each draft back, never by
   trusting the 200.
3. Submit each draft headlessly (`push.py submit`, accept terms, no captcha) and verify
   each flips to "Project submitted" rather than trusting the 200. Then file any
   one-per-entrant survey.

The worked tooling and the exact form recipe (per-form CSRF token, the optimistic-lock
`[version]` field, the positional sponsor-question indexing, the thumbnail multipart POST,
the finalization terms checkbox) live in `work/calle-submit/` and memory
`devpost-submission-api-recipe`. Reuse them for the next Devpost lane rather than
rebuilding: the content is per-project, the mechanism is not. One thumbnail note learned the
awkward way: the 16:9 YouTube thumbnails clip on Devpost's narrower project cards, so render
a card-safe 3:2 image (art inset from every edge) for this surface rather than reusing the
video thumbnail.

## Opportunity tracker (system of record for triage + follow-up)

Every triaged opportunity lives in the tracker at `work/opps/`, an interactive local web
app plus a CLI over the existing triage corpus (`work/_triage-cache/*.json`) and the status
store (`work/calendar-state.json`). It is to opportunities what `participations.md` is to
entries: the one place that answers what is GO, what is MAYBE, what we already skipped, what
needs action today (deadlines, submissions, re-checks).

Two axes per row. `verdict` (GO / MAYBE / SKIP) is the triage judgment and comes from the
corpus. `status` (new, researching, watching, owned, submitted, won, lost, dropped, merged)
is our engagement state and is editable. Whether we actually entered shows as a
`participated` flag, defaulting from the status and toggleable per row. `node
work/opps/opps.mjs dupes` surfaces duplicate clusters to merge; set the extra one to status
merged and the app hides it. A row needs action when: a deadline is near or
passed; a GO or owned row has no next action; a re-check is due; an owned row has gone stale.

Run it:
- `node work/opps/opps.mjs serve` then open http://127.0.0.1:7777 (localhost only, no auth
  because it never leaves the machine). Click a card to set status, next action, a deadline
  override, notes, links and tags. Edits write straight to `calendar-state.json`.
- `node work/opps/opps.mjs due` for the deadline + re-check queue in the terminal.
- `node work/opps/opps.mjs list --action` for everything needing attention.

Close the loop the moment a submission lands. When the operator says a submission is done
("submitted" or "mark it"), do these two steps before moving on, so the next target is picked
without rebuilding the deadline list by hand:
- Mark it: `node work/opps/opps.mjs set "<distinctive name>" --status submitted --next "await
  results" --due <results date if known>`. This writes only that one row to `calendar-state.json`.
- Show what is closing this week: `node work/opps/opps.mjs due --within 7`. Read the GO and MAYBE
  rows back to the operator with days left, prize and status, plus the `ending within Nd` tally so
  the MAYBE and SKIP counts show. Add `--all` to list the skips too.
Both go through `opps.mjs`, which reads via `board()` and writes one row at a time. Never run a full
`node work/calendar.mjs` board render (`--html`, `--all` or bare) just to peek at what is ending: it
persists every row of the skip corpus into `calendar-state.json` and bloated it from 421 to 2239 rows
once. Only `--set` is a safe calendar.mjs write.

Feed it, do not keep a second list:
- Before triaging a candidate run `node work/opps/opps.mjs check "<name>"`. Exit 0 means it
  is already tracked so skip the re-triage (this is how we stop re-checking the same dead
  rows). Exit 1 means it is genuinely new.
- Record a new verdict with `node work/opps/opps.mjs add --name .. --url .. --verdict GO
  --prize .. --deadline .. --notes ..`, or drop a scout findings JSON into
  `work/_triage-cache/`. Either way it shows up immediately.
- When a lane moves (start building, submit, win, drop) set it: `node work/opps/opps.mjs
  set "<name>" --status owned --next "..." --due 2026-09-01`.

Bounty PRs are tracked in the same app under the Bounties & PRs tab, backed by
`work/opps/prs.json`. PR state is pulled live from GitHub with `gh` (open/merged/closed,
review decision, CI, whether a maintainer replied after our last activity), so it never
drifts. Outcomes are handled explicitly: every PR resolves to in_flight, merged,
closed_unmerged or withdrawn, with a money ledger (expected bounty, claimed, paid) on top, so
the summary shows win rate, cash in flight, cash paid. Follow-up fires only on maintainer
activity we have not answered, on checks failing, on a merged PR whose bounty is unclaimed,
on a claimed bounty still unpaid. Never a proactive nudge (see [[no-proactive-followups-on-prs]]).
Refresh with `node work/opps/opps.mjs prs sync` or the Sync button; record money with
`node work/opps/opps.mjs prs set "<repo#num>" --program .. --bounty .. --outcome merged
--claimed --paid ..` so participations.md and this ledger agree.

Do not build a parallel tracker or paste triage results only into a memo. The daily
`work/calendar.mjs --html` board and this app read the same corpus and the same state, so
they always agree. `work/opps/lib/pipeline.mjs` is lifted from `calendar.mjs`; change the
dating or merge logic in one, mirror it in the other.

## Execution authority (standing)

These rules govern every target and every hackathon in this workspace, the same
way. They are not specific to one build.

zkasuran delegates execution end to end. Run the whole pipeline without pausing
for permission: build, test, commit, branch, push, version-bump, npm publish,
open and merge PRs in our own repos, open external bounty PRs (with the
disclosure and packet), regenerate evidence, and produce every content draft. Do
not stop a step merely because it is outward-facing or normally needs a nod. That
authority is granted. Act decisively, pick the sensible default and proceed.

This does not relax the non-negotiable principles. Real work only, AI disclosed
where the program requires it, green before submit, never fabricate that a human
reviewed code. zkasuran stays the owner of record and must be able to defend the
work, so always produce the defense packet (walkthrough, PR body, Q&A) even when
you open the PR. Delegating the typing and the submitting does not delegate the
honesty.

Ask only when the OUTCOME genuinely forks and you cannot settle it from the
request, the code, or these rules. Do not ask process or approval questions, and
do not re-confirm a routine outward step. Record each material decision in the
packet or `participations.md` so it can be reviewed after the fact.

One standing exception: the demo video. When a build reaches its submit stage, say so
and ask "Shall I build the demo video for `<project>`?", once, then wait. On yes, build
the whole thing without further questions. See **Demo videos** below.

Hard stops that still need a human, and only these:
- Anything that would break a non-negotiable principle (undisclosed AI where
  required, fake human review, deleting failing tests, a duplicate or low-effort
  PR).
- A destructive, unrecoverable action not implied by the task: force-push that
  rewrites already-published history, deleting a repo or someone else's data,
  account deletion or rename, rotating or exposing credentials. Regenerating or
  replacing the FLOP `did:key` is in this class: it orphans every signed post
  already on the service and cannot be undone.
- Spending real money or moving real funds.
For those, do everything up to the irreversible line and surface one ready
command.

Some final steps are blocked by interactive auth that cannot run headless: posting
to X or other socials, the hackathon submission form. Build all of it publish-ready
and hand off exactly those steps with the precise instructions. That is a tool
limit, not hesitation. Uploading the video to YouTube is **not** on that list any
more. The human signs in once and we publish it (see **Publishing to YouTube**).

## Content cadence (after every milestone)

Applies to every hackathon entry. After each shippable milestone (a version
published, a feature or PR merged, a PR opened, a bounty submitted), produce or
refresh the content in house style and keep it accurate to the shipped numbers.

- For a build with a public product and a community-impact component (the
  hackathon builds, e.g. Bitget, BNB, Mantle), produce the full set: a short post
  (one-shot, under 280 chars), a thread, the long-form article.
- For a bounty-PR contribution (e.g. unitaryHACK), the content that matters is the
  PR body, the submit packet and the disclosure, not a social thread. Do not force
  social posts on a bug-fix PR.

**Every finished project ships an article and an announce post, in one
click-to-copy HTML page.** This is not optional and it is not the same thing as the
X posts a milestone earns along the way. The moment a project is built, that page
exists, and it carries exactly four things:

1. **A title.** One line, specific, no colon-subtitle padding, no marketing verb.
   It names what the thing does or what was found, not what category it belongs to.
   Under 70 characters so it survives a card preview.
2. **The article.** The long-form piece in house style, accurate to the shipped
   numbers, with the measured figures and the links a reader can check. One copy
   button for the whole body, plus a formatting map naming which lines become
   headings and which numbers to bold, because the X Articles editor takes plain
   text and the human applies structure by hand.
3. **A 5:2 banner prompt.** The cover image, as a prompt the human pastes into an
   image model, never a generated file. **5:2 is the ratio the X Articles upload
   slot asks for: generate 3000 x 1200 and upload 1600 x 640.** The prompt
   describes the field only, plus a negative prompt. **Text never goes in the
   prompt**, because no image model sets type cleanly: the page carries the one or
   two lines of overlay text as their own copy blocks, to be placed afterwards in a
   vector tool. Say which palette or motif ties it to the project.
4. **The announce post.** The one-shot post that points at the article, under 280
   characters with a live count, tagging whatever account the programme scores.

The page is `CONTENT-<project>.html` in the lane, beside the build. It is publish
content, so it follows the click-to-copy rule below rather than living in a .md,
and it is separate from anything in `submit/`: the article is meant to be public,
so it carries no personal data, no form field ids and no keys.

Log each update in `work/CONTENT-LOG.md` (date, milestone, files touched, publish
status: drafted / posted). Content obeys the same writing-style rules and
disclosure posture as everything else. Quality is top tier every time, never
filler.

**Format: click-to-copy HTML, not .md.** Every content draft the human will
publish (X posts, threads, articles, form fills) ships as a self-contained
HTML file with a copy button per block (clipboard API, "copied" feedback) and
a char count on anything bound for X. Plain .md is fine for internal notes
(packets, triage, decision logs) but never for publishable content.

**Anything the human has to paste into somebody else's box is click-to-copy HTML,
always, with no exceptions.** Submissions, registrations, form fills, profile
fields, grant applications, bounty claim forms, a hackathon submission portal, a
demo video upload: every one of them ships as a self-contained HTML page with **one
copy button per field**, because a field is what the human pastes and a field is
therefore the unit. A markdown table of values is not a deliverable. Values printed
in a chat message are not a deliverable. A .md file the human has to select text
out of is not a deliverable. Each block carries the exact field name as the
receiving form spells it (`liveAppUrl`, not "the app link"), and a live character
count against that field's real limit wherever one exists.

The page also carries what the values alone cannot: the URL of the form, the order
the fields appear in, which ones are dropdowns rather than text, any pre-submit gate
(a repo that must be public, a URL that must return 200 to an anonymous fetch), and
the one-line record of what was already filed so a re-submission edits in place
instead of creating a duplicate row. If the submission ran headlessly, the page
still exists, because the human may have to correct it in the UI later and should
not have to reconstruct the values.

**Submission and form-fill HTML lives in `submit/` inside the project, and never
ships to GitHub.** The click-to-copy pages the human fills a submission or
registration form from (a `SUBMIT-*.html`, the registration fill, any form fill)
are internal tooling that carries private data: the author's real name and email,
the exact form field ids, an instruction to paste an API key. Put them in a
`submit/` folder inside the lane's own repo folder so they travel with the build,
then add `/submit/` to that repo's `.gitignore` so they are never pushed. A public
hackathon repo that contains our form-fill HTML leaks personal data and the
submission internals, so this is not optional. Before the repo flips public, prove
it: `git check-ignore submit/` returns the path and `git status` does not list the
folder. The render outputs get the same posture, kept in the lane and out of the
code repo by `.gitignore`: the finished `DEMO-*.mp4` and the `upload-<id>/` package.

The demo video is content too, but it has its own rule and its own trigger. See
**Demo videos** below: offer it when the build is done, build it on yes.

## Frontends: read landing.md first

Every website or landing page we build, for a hackathon or anything else, follows `~/.claude/landing.md`. Read
it in full before you start. Defaults, always: light AND dark mode (system preference plus a persisted toggle,
no flash of the wrong theme), a category top-menu whose submenus open on hover, focus and tap and classify the
site, plus a product-first hero that states what the thing does with its action on screen. Judges skim, so it
must be catchy and straight to the point, never a report or wall-of-text, never everything piled on one page.
After shipping, append what won or failed to `landing.md` under Winning flavours.

## Hardened to ship (every submission, no exceptions)

A submission is not done when it works. It is done when a hostile input, a hostile reviewer and a hostile
network have all been tried against it and lost. The reference build is `work/hailjury` (`./verify.sh`,
`SECURITY.md`); copy its gate rather than re-inventing one. Every item below is required, and the packet
says which command proved it.

1. **One release gate, one command.** A `verify.sh` at the repo root runs every check below in order,
   `set -euo pipefail`, and prints `ALL GREEN` only at the end. CI runs the same script, so a judge and a
   reviewer get the same verdict. A check that is not in the gate does not exist.
2. **Lint with warnings as errors.** `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` (plus the wasm target when
   there is one), `tsc` strict with `noUnused*`, `cargo fmt --check`. Zero warnings, not "only the usual ones".
3. **No panics on untrusted input.** Library code that parses anything a stranger can send (memos, ledgers,
   files, JSON, URLs) denies `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic`, `unreachable` and `todo` outside tests
   (`#![cfg_attr(not(test), deny(clippy::unwrap_used, clippy::expect_used, clippy::panic))]`) and forbids
   `unsafe`. Every failure is an `Err` with a message, never an abort that takes everyone else down.
4. **Adversarial and property tests, not just happy paths.** Random bytes into every parser, random
   inputs into every pure function with the invariants asserted (conservation of value, bounds, order
   independence), and one named test per attack in the threat model. Keep them fast enough to run every
   time (optimise dependencies in the test profile) or they stop being run.
5. **Ceilings on everything untrusted.** Sizes, counts, string lengths, file sizes, response sizes and
   network timeouts, as named constants in one place. A hostile input must never exhaust memory or CPU.
6. **Normalise before you compare.** Case, padding, whitespace and encoding variants of one thing must not
   count twice or bypass a check. Normalise at the boundary, then deduplicate.
7. **Never trust a source because it is ours or because it is popular.** Verify signatures, pin the
   expected key or chain and check the answer matches the question (the round asked for, the id asked for).
   Re-verify our own published fixtures and anything read back from browser storage before rendering it.
8. **Secrets never in argv, logs or URLs.** Seed and key files with a permission check, or an env var.
   Keep keys and tickets out of query strings. Zeroise where the library supports it.
9. **Supply chain is part of the build.** Pin every direct dependency exactly, commit both lockfiles, and
   gate on `cargo audit`, `cargo deny` (licences, sources, wildcards) and `npm audit` at 0 findings.
   Check every new dependency name for typosquats before adding it.
10. **Web hardening on every site.** A strict CSP generated at build time (`default-src 'none'`, scripts by
    hash, `connect-src` listing the exact hosts), escaped rendering of any data shown as HTML, an error
    boundary so one view cannot blank the app, fetch timeouts, and a `_headers` file (frame-ancestors,
    nosniff, referrer, HSTS, permissions). Details in `landing.md` under Hardening.
11. **A threat model in the repo.** `SECURITY.md` with one row per attacker and attack, the defence and the
    file that holds it, plus an honest Known limits list. If a defence has no test, the row says so.
12. **Prove it end to end in the real runtime.** Drive the built artifact the way a judge will: the CLI
    on a real fixture (honest input passes, tampered input exits non-zero), the site in headless Chrome
    in both themes at 390 and 1360 wide with zero console errors and zero CSP violations, and every
    tamper or failure path actually exercised. Unit tests alone are not evidence.
13. **Say what is simulated.** Anything mocked or not yet live is labelled in the product and the README,
    never implied to be real. A judge who finds an unlabelled mock stops trusting everything else.

## The GitHub README (every repo we ship, built like a landing page)

The README is the first page a judge opens and often the only one, so it is designed, not written up. It
must be beautiful, complete and informative, and it follows the same product-first rules as a site
(`landing.md`, section "The GitHub README"). Reference: `work/hailjury/README.md`. Template:
`~/.claude/templates/readme/README.template.md`.

Required, in this order:

1. **A banner** in both GitHub themes: `<picture>` with `prefers-color-scheme` sources pointing at
   `docs/assets/banner-dark.svg` and `banner-light.svg`. Hand-made SVG (product name, tagline, one
   accent, one brand mark), never a stock image, rendered once in headless Chrome to check it.
2. **A nav row** (live demo first, then try it, how it works, security, spec) and a short row of
   static shields.io badges that state facts we can prove (test count, 0 audit findings, licence, stack).
   No dynamic CI badge while the repo is private: it renders broken to every anonymous viewer.
3. **The one-paragraph pitch** saying what it does, with the single number that matters in bold, plus a
   "why now" line backed by a fact we verified.
4. **A real product screenshot** under the pitch, captured from the live deploy at deviceScaleFactor 2,
   in both themes via `<picture>`. Never a mockup.
5. **Try it in 60 seconds:** a numbered table of what to click and what you will see, against the live URL.
6. **How it works:** a Mermaid sequence or flow diagram (GitHub renders it) plus 3 to 5 numbered
   sentences, then a 2 x 2 screenshot grid with one-line captions.
7. **The reference tables the product needs:** use cases, the privacy or trust model, what the audit
   or verifier checks, and **What is real and what is simulated**. That last one is never optional.
8. **Architecture:** a Mermaid diagram of the components and the external systems.
9. **Run it locally and the CLI or API quickstart:** copy-pasteable, tested, with secrets via files.
10. **Built to be attacked:** a security summary linking `SECURITY.md`, and the one-command gate
    (`./verify.sh`) with what it runs.
11. **Repository layout, roadmap (checked and unchecked) and licence**, with the exact SPDX id.

Rules: every number in it is measured; every link resolves; images live in `docs/assets/` with
optimised PNGs (keep each under about 500 KB); house outward-words style; no wall of prose, since
every section is a heading, one or two sentences and a table, diagram or image. Before the repo flips
public, open the README as an anonymous viewer and confirm every image and link renders.

## Demo videos (one consolidated rule, every project, no exceptions)

A demo video is a quarter of most rubrics and it is the piece that used to block the
human at the end. This section is the whole rule: when to make one, what it must be,
how to build it and what to check.

### Offer it, then build it

The moment a project is feature-complete and moving into its submit stage, say the
build is done and ask one line: **"Shall I build the demo video for `<project>`?"**
Then wait. On yes, build it end to end, including the brief and the gates, without
further questions. On no, or on silence, do not build it and move on.

This is the one standing exception to "do not ask process or approval questions" in
**Execution authority**. Ask once per project, never per step, and never ask again for
the same project unless the video needs a rebuild for a reason worth a sentence.

Everything else on this page still applies. Rendering costs minutes of wall clock and
turns, so it is the user's call whether a given project earns one.

### Every video gets its own theme

One theme per video, never reused across projects. The roster is `PALETTES` in
`work/calle-video/theme.py`: gradient ends, accent, highlighter ink, three blobs and a
field shape (`vertical` ramp, `diagonal` ramp, `radial` pool), so two videos differ in
the shape of the light as well as its colour. Claim a free theme in
`work/VIDEO-THEMES.md` before building and record it after. `preflight.py` prints who
holds what and fails on a collision. When the free list runs out, add a palette rather
than doubling up: bright gradient ends, an accent dark enough to read on the near-white
panel, a mark pale enough to multiply over dark ink, and a check frame before
committing to it.

The same unique-per-demo discipline covers the **thumbnail**. Its design, not just
its colours, is built fresh for each demo: no two demos ship the same thumbnail
layout. See the thumbnail rule under **The upload package**.

### Built for the project it is showing

Pick the scenes from what that project actually produces and let each video have its
own spine. A CI gate earns pipeline panels drawn from a real run with real exit codes,
a coordinator earns the availability grid drawn from its real ledger, a delegated
errand earns the report document and the verbatim transcript. Pouring three different
projects into one terminal template is a tell that nobody looked at the work.

Renderers in the kit: `scene.py` terminal window, `panel.py` step lists and chip rows,
`doc.py` report document and chat bubbles, `grid.py` party-by-option matrix, `code.py`
source file with light syntax colour, `cards.py` caption cards. Each returns `image`,
`window` and `boxes`, so one painter drives all of them and a new scene type is one
renderer plus one branch in `prepare()`.

### What a shipped video has

- **Bright, colourful, generated.** The field is drawn by `bg.py` and cached, never a
  downloaded image, so there is no image licence to defend.
- **The recording window floats on that field.** Near-white panel, window chrome, soft
  drop shadow, dark ink. Dense monospace stays on the light panel: the brightness lives
  around the text, never behind it. Legible at 720p.
- **Zoom follows the words.** Every narration cue names the line it is about
  (`{"text": ..., "focus": "substring"}`) and the frame eases into that region while
  the cue plays, then back out. No aimless drifting. The box anchors to the left of the
  text and holds the whole window on any axis where it fits.
- **The line being spoken is marked.** A highlighter sweep wipes across it in time with
  the cue, multiplied into the page like real ink so coloured text keeps its colour.
  The lines worth marking are usually the refusals, and a refusal must stay red.
- **A custom cursor.** It travels to the marked line with easing, with a soft shadow
  and a click ripple when it lands.
- **A progress bar**, drawn on the delivered frame so a zoom can never crop it.
- **Whatever a cue points at is on screen when it is spoken.** Content lands at a
  steady cadence and a focused row is revealed immediately. A cue that talks about a
  line the reveal has not reached yet loses its zoom, its marker and its cursor.
- **Audio first.** Cues are synthesised and measured, then segments are sized to the
  words, so nothing drifts and nothing is clipped. Loudness -16 LUFS integrated, true
  peak under -1.5 dBTP, measured on the finished file. Cue files are keyed by a digest
  of the words, so an edited line is always re-read and an unchanged one is never paid
  for twice.
- **Music is required. It is ducked under the voice.** Sidechain it, fade it in and
  out, then only ship a track whose licence we can point at. The house track is
  `~/Downloads/joyinsound-no-copyright-music-398375.mp3` (no-copyright), passed as
  `MUSIC=` to `build.py`. A silent cut is an unfinished cut: if the track is missing,
  find a licensed one rather than shipping without. Name the track and its licence in
  the brief.
- **The product and its source are both on screen.** Every video carries at least one
  `web` scene captured from the **live deployed URL** the submission cites, plus at least
  one `code` or `term` scene showing the source or the build that produces it. A cut that
  is all terminal never proves the thing is reachable by a judge. A cut that is all
  website never proves it is real. Both, every time. Show the URL as text on screen so a
  viewer can type it.
- **Everything on screen is real.** Commands run for real and the raw stdout is kept in
  `artifacts/`; panels, grids, reports and code cards read a real file or a real run.
  Only a viewport is shown. Never retype output and never mock a panel.
- **The honesty labels stay on screen.** Staged reproduction, no real call placed, fake
  server, whatever is true for that shot, for the whole shot.
- **Length and platform come from the program's rules**, and the build refuses to
  finish over its cap.

### The upload package

A rendered mp4 is not a deliverable. The deliverable is everything the upload form asks
for, built and gated the same way the video is, so the human's only job is paste and
click. Every video ships one, in `work/<lane>/upload-<id>/`, generated by
`python3 upload.py projects/<id>.json`.

**`UPLOAD-<id>.html` is the package.** One self-contained page, opened once, with every
field beside a copy button and nothing that needs a second document open. It carries, in
order: the title, the full description with the chapters already inlined, the tags, the
chapter list on its own, **the thumbnail embedded twice, at full size and again at 168
pixels wide**, the captions as a copy block, **every in and out time the build measured**,
the rest of the form field by field, the gates, then where the URL goes once it exists.
Each text block shows a live character count against its limit.

The sidecar files exist only because YouTube wants real files to upload. The page offers
both as downloads anyway:

| Artifact | What it is | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UPLOAD-<id>.html` | the whole upload in one click-to-copy page | title under 100, description under 5000, tags under 500, every block present |
| `thumbnail.png` or `.jpg` | a unique design per demo on the video's own theme, never a downloaded image and never a frame grab with text pasted on | 3840x2160, 16:9, under 2 MB so it uploads from a phone too, then looked at by eye |
| `captions.srt` | every narration cue with the exact in and out times the build measured | cue count matches the project file, last out time inside the duration, no cue shorter than 0.8s |
| `chapters.txt` | the scene table as timestamps | first is `0:00`, at least 3, each at least 10 seconds, ascending |

**In and out times are measured, never re-derived.** `build.py` writes
`artifacts/<id>/timing.json` as it renders and `upload.py` reads it, so a timestamp in the
page is a timestamp in the delivered file. The page shows two tables from it: the scenes
with their in, out and duration, each against the chapter it opens and with the climaxes
shaded, then all narration cues with their SRT in and out times. That table is also the
caption file, so the two cannot disagree.

Those limits are YouTube's own, not ours: **title 100 characters, description 5000
characters, thumbnail 3840x2160 recommended with a 640px minimum width and 16:9, and
chapters must start at `0:00`, number at least three, then run at least 10 seconds each.**
A description that carries chapter timestamps overrides YouTube's automatic ones, which is
why we write them rather than letting it guess. Tags carry no published limit and YouTube
says they play a minimal role, so the 500 character ceiling is a house convention to stop
keyword stuffing rather than a quoted rule.

The page is HTML with a copy button per block because it is content the human publishes,
which is the same rule as every other draft (see **Content cadence**). The form fields it
spells out rather than leaves to memory: the visibility (**public, never unlisted**, a
submission that links an unlisted video is a broken link to a judge who is not signed in),
the category, the video and caption language, the "not made for kids" answer, the altered
content answer, the recording date, the playlist, the measured length, plus the two file
names. Each copies on its own, because some of them are typed into a box rather than picked
from a menu.

The description is not a blurb. In order: what the product does in two or three sentences,
what each integration actually contributes, the live links, one line saying what was newly
built during the program, the chapter timestamps, the honesty paragraph naming exactly what
is real and what is staged in this cut, the measured numbers a judge can check, the licence,
and the AI disclosure with the synthesised-narration line. Anything asserted there must
already be true in the brief.

The words live in an `upload` block in the project file, never in the page and never only in
the brief, so there is one place to edit them and the brief cannot drift from the package.
Re-run `upload.py` after any change to the words or the timing.

The thumbnail is generated by `thumb.py` on the project's palette: the field, the product
name, one line of claim and at most one number. No frame grab, no stock photo, no face, no
arrow, no red circle. It has to read at 168 pixels wide in a sidebar, which is why the page
renders it at that size next to the full one: if the headline stops reading there, it fails
in the page rather than on the channel.

The thumbnail is a **unique design per demo**, not the theme recoloured onto one fixed
layout. Give each demo its own composition: where the product name, the claim and the single
number sit on the field, the focal shape, the crop, built for that project the way its scenes
are. No two demos ship the same thumbnail layout. When `thumb.py`'s layouts start to repeat,
add a new one rather than doubling up, and look at the free frame by eye before committing,
the same discipline as the per-video theme. `preflight.py` should fail a thumbnail layout
already claimed by another demo, the way it fails a reused palette.

This applies to **every video, with no exceptions and no grandfathering**. A thumbnail, a
caption file and chapter timestamps are deliverables of the same rank as the mp4: a cut
without them is not finished, whatever its render date. `upload.py` refuses a project that
has no `upload` block. That refusal is the reminder rather than a bug. Older videos
built before this rule do not get a pass: if one is about to be uploaded, add the `upload`
block and generate the package first. `upload.py` also needs `artifacts/<id>/timing.json`,
which only `build.py` writes, so a video whose timing was never recorded has to be rebuilt
rather than hand-timed. That rebuild is the cost of having shipped it unfinished. It is
cheaper than a judge opening a video with no chapters and no captions.

### Build order

```bash
cd work/calle-video                     # or a copy of the kit in the lane
python3 scaffold.py <id> <app-dir> "The headline."   # claims a free theme, writes a project file that already builds
python3 preflight.py projects/*.json    # every segment drawn, every focus needle resolved, themes unique
python3 frame.py projects/<id>.json 27 62 78   # single frames at the beats, painter warmed
MUSIC=<licensed track> python3 build.py projects/<id>.json
python3 upload.py projects/<id>.json    # thumbnail, captions, chapters, the click-to-copy fields
cp out/<id>.mp4 ../<lane>/DEMO-<id>.mp4       # the finished file lives with its project
python3 manifest.py projects/*.json     # regenerate the narration manifest after any wording change
```

The scaffold is a starting point, not a template: replace its middle with scenes drawn
from what the project actually produces. Both gates cost seconds and a render costs
minutes, so never skip them. `AUDIO_ONLY=1` reuses the rendered picture and rebuilds
only the sound. `upload.py` reads the timing the build measured rather than re-deriving it,
so it has to run after a build and has to be re-run after any wording or timing change.

The kit's `out/` is a build directory, so the finished file does not stay there. File it
with the project it shows as `work/<lane>/DEMO-<id>.mp4`, the upload package beside it as
`work/<lane>/upload-<id>/`, then add its row to `work/VIDEOS.md` (file, measured length and
size, theme, where it gets uploaded). Build scratch, the captured stdout and the segment
clips, stays in `work/calle-video/artifacts/<id>/`.

### The brief

Ship one file per project, `work/<project>/CODEX-VIDEO-BRIEF.md`, so the video can be
rebuilt and defended without any other context. It carries, in one file: what shipped
(paths, length, size, measured loudness) and the asset state behind it; how to rebuild
it; the scene table with real in and out times naming the climaxes that must never lose
time; the complete narration cue list with real start seconds; every on-screen string
verbatim; the locked lines that must survive, real output only, never invented; the
honesty framing; the verification gates with expected numbers; and the upload step, which
points at the generated `upload-<id>/` package rather than repeating it, plus anything
about the upload a generator cannot know.

The brief is the source of truth for the words and the package is the rendering of them.
If the two disagree, the brief is wrong or `upload.py` was not re-run, and either way the
build is not shippable.

### Gates before upload

ffprobe duration and streams, loudness pass on the finished file, em dash grep on
narration and captions, locked-lines check against the captured stdout, and a frame
pulled out of the finished mp4 at each climax and actually looked at.

Four more that follow from the rules above, each of which has been shipped wrong at least
once, so check them rather than assuming:

- **Music is present.** ffprobe the audio, then confirm the build logged the track name
  instead of `no music`. A silent ship is the default failure when `MUSIC=` is forgotten.
- **The live URL scene resolves.** The `web` scene captured a real page, then that same URL
  fetched anonymously returns 200. A scene shot against localhost or a stale deploy is a
  fabricated claim about something a judge will click.
- **The thumbnail and the caption file both exist** and came out of `upload.py`, not a
  frame grab and not hand timing. The thumbnail is a design unique to this demo, not a
  reused layout, so `preflight.py` must not report its layout as already claimed.
- **A source or build scene is in the cut.** Grep the project file for a `code` or `term`
  segment. All-website cuts prove nothing about the code.

Then the upload package, which has its own gates because a broken description or an
illegible thumbnail costs the same rubric points a bad cut does: the four character and
chapter limits above checked against the generated text rather than eyeballed, the caption
file's last out time inside the measured duration, the thumbnail opened and looked at at
full size **and** shrunk to sidebar width to confirm it still reads, and every URL the
description cites fetched anonymously for a 200. A description that links a private repo or
a dead Pages site is worse than no description.

Then log the build in `work/CONTENT-LOG.md` with the theme, the measured numbers and the
publish
status.

### Publishing to YouTube (we do it, the human only signs in)

The YouTube Data API is out. Since 28 July 2020, every upload from an API project that has
not passed YouTube's compliance audit is locked private, with no appeal
(support.google.com/youtube/answer/7300965). So we drive YouTube Studio in a real Chrome:

```bash
bin/yt-chrome.sh       # one Chrome, 127.0.0.1:9333, profile ~/.cache/yt-studio-chrome
                       # -> the human signs in to the channel's Google account in that window, once
python3 bin/yt-studio-upload.py upload  work/<lane>/yt.json e1 e2 e3 e4 e5 e0   # trailer last
python3 bin/yt-studio-upload.py verify  work/<lane>/yt.json   # oEmbed 200 signed out = public
python3 bin/yt-studio-upload.py drafts  work/<lane>/yt.json   # catch retry leftovers
python3 bin/yt-studio-upload.py upload  work/<lane>/yt.json e2:<videoId>        # finish a stuck draft
python3 bin/yt-studio-upload.py thumbs  work/<lane>/yt.json [e1 …]   # swap thumbnails on published videos
```

`yt.json` holds the channel id (`UC…`, read off the Studio URL after sign-in) and, for each
video, the master's path, title, description (with the chapters already expanded),
tags and thumbnail. All of those come out of the upload package, never retyped. The
script lints YouTube's limits before it touches the browser. It refuses a title over
100, a description over 5000, tags over 500, any `<` or `>`, a leftover `{placeholder}`
and a thumbnail over 2 MB. Video ids go to `yt-ids.json` beside the config. Put them
into the site and the README, rebuild, redeploy, then fetch every page anonymously.

Uploads are fast (a 360 MB master took about a minute). The traps are all in Studio. Each
of these cost a retry on Zero to Shielded (2026-10-04). The script now handles each one:

- **One connection for the whole batch.** A second `connect_over_cdp` after a run that
  left a busy tab hung for minutes. Pass every episode in one `upload` call.
- **Files over 50 MB go in through raw CDP** (`DOM.setFileInputFiles`). Playwright refuses
  to transfer them to a browser it did not launch.
- **Publish only after "Uploading" clears, then wait for "Video published".** Closing the tab
  4 s after Publish left five videos as drafts. A draft looks published in the list, but its
  row has no `/video/<id>/edit` link. `drafts` shows it.
- **Never press Escape in the dialog.** It closes the whole upload, not the sub-menu. Close
  tabs with `run_before_unload=False`.
- **Subtitles need the video language set first.** The in-dialog SRT upload is flaky, so it
  is opt-in (`SUBS=1`). If it fails, add `captions.srt` afterwards under Subtitles, then
  "Upload file", "With timing". Without our file YouTube makes automatic captions, which
  mishear product names.
- **A custom thumbnail needs a phone-verified channel.** If the thumbnail step fails, check
  that first. To confirm a swap went live, compare `i.ytimg.com/vi/<id>/hqdefault.jpg`
  against the new file. A plain HTML page with the font embedded as a data URI renders a clearer
  thumbnail than a drawn one: a `file://` font silently falls back to Arial.
- **If Chrome itself dies** (it did once, `bad_variant_access`), rerun `bin/yt-chrome.sh`. The
  profile keeps the sign-in.
- **Check the port before you serve.** Something else on this machine was listening on
  8765, so local checks hit the wrong server. Run them on a free port with `--base`.

Deleting retry drafts is the human's call: it is their channel and it cannot be undone.
List them in the handoff with their ids.

## Lessons from entering these things (`LESSONS.md`)

`LESSONS.md` at this workspace root is the competing playbook: reusable principles for deciding whether
to enter, building toward a rubric, hitting submission gates, and reading a result. House rules say what
we always do. Lessons say what happened when we did it.

**Read it at triage**, before deciding whether to enter and before deciding how to position, alongside
`~/.claude/LESSONS.md` for the engineering half.

**It is organised by WHEN YOU NEED IT**, from triage through to result, never by date. **Never append a
dated entry to the end.** A diary of past entries is not something anyone reads under deadline pressure.

### How to write one

1. **Lead with the principle, in language that transfers to the next program.** "Falsify the gap before
   you build on it" generalises. "8004scan indexed 10,174 agents" is the evidence for it, not the
   lesson.
2. **Put the incident underneath as a `>` blockquote, one or two lines.** Program names can stay where
   they carry weight, but the rule above must stand without them.
3. **File it under the decision point where someone would need it**: entering, building, submitting,
   or after the result.
4. **Merge, do not accumulate.** Sharpen an existing entry and add your evidence to its blockquote
   rather than writing a near-duplicate.
5. **Keep it scannable.** This gets read the day before a deadline.

### When to write

* a submission was rejected, disqualified or scored badly, and the stated reason is known
* a program's rules, rubric, gates or review behaviour differed from what we assumed at triage
* a deadline, form, upload, visibility flip or claim step nearly slipped or did slip
* a rival or incumbent turned out to already do the thing we were positioning as new
* a placement or payout landed, win or loss

Then update the **outcome ledger** at the bottom with the date, program, entry, outcome and the one line
that actually decided it. A result with no cause is a scoreboard. With the cause it is strategy, and it
is what makes the next triage a judgement instead of a guess.

Keep the routing clean so none of the three files rots:

| Scope | Goes in |
|---|---|
| true of hackathons, bounty programs, judging, submissions | `LESSONS.md` here |
| true regardless of project, including personal and local work | `~/.claude/LESSONS.md` |
| true of one target only | that lane's `.hq/MEMORY.md` |

`participations.md` stays the per-entry record of what was submitted, under which account, and what came
back. `LESSONS.md` is the generalisation drawn from those records. Record the entry in one and the
lesson in the other; do not let either become the other.

## Repository visibility (private while building, public to submit)

Every repo we create for a hackathon build starts **private**. It stays private
through the whole build and flips public only when the lane reaches its submission
stage. `gh repo create <name> --private` is the default and `--public` is the
exception that needs a reason.

Why: an unfinished build is not evidence, it is a preview for rivals. In the
skill and agent competitions the repo often IS the submission, so a public repo
during the build hands the whole entry to anyone scanning the org. Half-built work
also reads worse to a judge who wanders in early than the same work does when it
is finished, documented and gated.

The flip is not optional and it is not cosmetic. A submitted writeup that links a
private repo is broken for every judge who clicks it, which voids the
reproducibility claim the entry rests on, and programs that expect competition
code to be shared publicly can read a private repo as non-compliance.

So, at submission stage, in this order:

1. Flip it: `gh api -X PATCH repos/<owner>/<repo> -F private=false`.
2. Verify as a stranger, not as us. An anonymous fetch of the repo page must
   return 200, and every URL the submission actually cites must resolve, including
   raw file and blob links to any asset the writeup or the video description names.
   Our own `gh` calls are authenticated and will pass either way, so they prove
   nothing here.
3. Record the flip and the verification in the lane's resume log or state doc,
   with the exact command, so a later session can tell a deliberate private repo
   from one that was left private by accident.

Two standing exceptions:

- **Fork repos stay public.** A PR from a private fork breaks the upstream pull
  request. `zkasuran/skillsbench` is public for exactly that reason and must not
  be flipped private while its PR is open.
- **A repo the program requires public from the start** follows the program's
  rule, not this one. Note that in the lane ledger when it happens.

While a build repo is private, the lane must carry the flip as an OPEN item with
its trigger and its hard deadline, because a private repo at judging time is the
same as no submission.
