## 4. Trails, Graph, Brain

Prize scope (confirmed from the hackathon page): "Best Use of Entire" rewards the most creative use of Checkpoints, Graph, or Brain. Trails is not named in the prize criteria, so treat it as optional polish, not a scored feature.

### Checkpoints
Covered above. Glossary: "A save point for your work. Entire creates checkpoints around agent activity and links committed ones to Git commits."

### Graph (confirmed, except where noted)
`entire-graph` is a plugin that maps your repo's code and relationships so an agent can locate implementations and trace what calls what. Prereqs: Entire CLI 0.10.0+, Git 2.36+, a local git repo, and an agent that reads `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`.
```bash
entire plugin install graph
entire graph version
entire graph init-agents --repo .   # writes .entire/graph-agent.md, updates AGENTS.md & CLAUDE.md
git add .entire/graph-agent.md AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Enable entire-graph"

Glossary has no entry, but the overview defines it as shared, repo-resident agent memory: find earlier decisions, save lessons, hand context to an agent before it starts. entire brain init-agents              # writes .entire/agent-guide.md, references it in AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md

Glossary: a Trail is "Entire's unit of work, covering one branch and one pull request from one intent to shipped code." ## 5. Using checkpoints meaningfully in PriorProof (important correction)

Your example "checkpoint the parsed chart after extraction and the coverage state before packet assembly, so a run resumes without re-reading the chart" describes runtime state-snapshotting of the deployed prior-auth agent. Entire does not do that. Entire checkpoints are development-time pairings of a coding-agent session with a git commit. It will not natively snapshot your Next.js app's execution state on Vercel. State that plainly in planning so the submission narrative stays honest.

Two clean ways to make the idea real and still win "Best Use of Entire":

- Map each pipeline stage to its own checkpoint during the build. Build chart-extraction, coverage-lookup, and packet-assembly each in a dedicated agent session and commit each as its own checkpoint with a descriptive message. A judge then runs `entire checkpoint explain <ID>` or opens the commit URL and sees the reasoning, prompts, and diffs behind each stage. This is the most direct, confirmed, meaningful use, and it is exactly what the checkpoint link in the submission should showcase. Pair it with Graph (so the agent navigates the growing codebase cheaply) and Brain (persist decisions like "coverage rules live in X, prove-or-refuse threshold is Y" via `entire brain remember`, recalled in later sessions). Using all three is the strongest claim for the prize.
- Implement the runtime resume as a PriorProof app feature in its own right (write parsed-chart JSON and coverage state to disk or a store, resume from there), which is good engineering independent of Entire. If you want an Entire angle on the actual agent run, Entire's confirmed resume primitive is cross-session, not cross-request: `entire session resume` / Resume Sessions continues a stopped coding session or hands work between agents. Tell the "resume without re-reading the chart" story as your app feature; do not attribute it to Entire checkpoints.

Submission pointer (confirmed): neatHack requires an accessible checkpoint link + ID. Use the checkpoint for your most illustrative stage commit (for example the coverage/packet-assembly commit), give its entire.io/gh/... URL and its `Entire-Checkpoint:` ULID.

## PriorProof × neatlogs: TypeScript/Node instrumentation

### 1. Package name and version (CONFIRMED)

- npm package: **`neatlogs`** (unscoped). Current version **1.1.28**, license MIT, `engines.node >=18.0.0`.
- Source repo: **github.com/neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript** (the npm `neatlogs` package IS this TS SDK; the Python SDK is a separate `neatlogs` on PyPI).
- It is **OpenTelemetry-native** (depends on `@opentelemetry/*` and `protobufjs`); it exports OTLP-proto spans over HTTP.
- Related package: `@neatlogs/wizard` (v0.1.11), the `npx @neatlogs/wizard` auto-setup CLI. Not needed if you instrument by hand.

```bash
npm install neatlogs
```

Sources: [neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript README](https://github.com/neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript) · npm registry `registry.npmjs.org/neatlogs` (dist-tags.latest = 1.1.28) · [hackathon setup guide](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/neatlogs-setup-guide.html).

### 2. Initialization (CONFIRMED)

- Env var: **`NEATLOGS_API_KEY`**. There is **no project id for the SDK** — the API key itself selects the project.
- Two keys exist in the dashboard and they are not interchangeable: use the **Project API key** (the top one) for the Node SDK. The **HTTP ingest key starting with `nlw_`** is for raw HTTP / the browser SDK only; passing `nlw_` to the Node SDK returns 401. (`NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` + `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` exist only for reading traces back via the CLI/public API, not for ingest.)

```typescript
import { init, shutdown, wrapOpenAI } from 'neatlogs';
import OpenAI from 'openai';

await init({ apiKey: process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY, workflowName: 'my-first-app' });
const client = wrapOpenAI(new OpenAI());
// ...
await shutdown(); // flushes anything still queued
```

Key `init()` options (from the README `InitOptions` table): `apiKey` (default `process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY`, export disabled if unset), `workflowName`, `userId`, `tags`, `metadata`, `debug`, `disableExport`, `sampleRate`, `captureLogs` (needed for `log()`), `endpoint` (default `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`; SDK posts to `/v1/traces` and `/v1/logs`), `registerShutdownHandlers` (default true). Ingest uses header `x-api-key` + gzip (confirmed in `src/core/client.ts`). Must be wrapped in an `async function main()`; no top-level await.

### 3. Trace for one run + spans per step (CONFIRMED)

**`init()` does not monkeypatch.** You get spans two ways, and you can mix them:

- `span(options, fn)` — higher-order wrapper; returns an instrumented version of `fn` that auto-captures input, output, timing, errors. `kind` is required.
- `trace(options, fn)` — inline; runs the callback immediately, passes it the live OTel span, auto-captures `options.input` and the callback's return value, and creates a root trace when `sessionId` is set. Nesting is automatic: a `span()`/`trace()` called inside another becomes its child via OTel context.

`SpanKind` values (for `span()`): `WORKFLOW, AGENT, CHAIN, TOOL, RETRIEVER, EMBEDDING, MCP_TOOL, GUARDRAIL`. `trace()` additionally accepts `LLM, RERANKER, VECTOR_STORE` plus `GUARDRAIL, EVALUATOR`.

Mapping for PriorProof's five steps: policy criterion parse → `CHAIN`; evidence lookup → `RETRIEVER` (or `TOOL`); evidence match → `CHAIN`; criterion decision → `AGENT` or `CHAIN`; refusal → `GUARDRAIL`. One agent run = one `WORKFLOW` root.

Inputs/outputs attach automatically (`captureInput`/`captureOutput` default `true` on `span()`; `trace()` captures `input` and the returned value). Extra data: `setAttribute()` on the span, `log('msg {x}', { x })` for timestamped steps (requires `captureLogs: true`), and `setTraceOutput(value)` to override the trace's displayed final output (stamped as `neatlogs.trace.output` on the root).

**Marking a step failed (CONFIRMED, with an important nuance):**
- The built-in mechanism is to **throw** inside the wrapped fn/callback. The SDK catches it, calls `span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR, message })` and `span.recordException(err)`, then rethrows (`src/core/context.ts` lines 457-465; `src/decorators/base.ts` lines 291-297).
- Nuance that matters for a prove-or-refuse agent: **`span()` forces `setStatus(OK)` on success** (`base.ts:242`), so it will overwrite a manual error status if the fn returns normally. **`trace()` does not reset status on success**, so to mark a step failed *without aborting the run* (e.g. a refusal that is a business outcome, not a crash) you must use `trace()` and call `span.setStatus({ code: 2 /* ERROR */ })` + `span.recordException(...)` on the span the callback receives, then return normally. My wrapper below uses `trace()` for exactly this reason.

### 5. LLM wrapper vs manual, and Vercel (CONFIRMED + one strong inference)

- **Both.** Explicit LLM-client wrappers exist and are **not** auto-instrumentation — you call them yourself: `wrapOpenAI`, `wrapAnthropic`, `wrapAzureOpenAI`, `wrapBedrock`, `wrapGoogleGenAI`/`wrapVertexAI`, `wrapAISDK` (Vercel AI SDK, import `neatlogs/ai`), plus framework hooks (`langchainHandler()`, `openaiAgentsProcessor()`, `wrapMastra`, `wrapClaudeAgentSDK`, etc.). Manual spans via `span()`/`trace()` cover everything that is not an LLM call (your evidence lookup, matching, decision logic). For PriorProof you will mostly want manual spans for the deterministic steps and a wrapper around whichever LLM client parses criteria.
- **Server-side on Vercel: works in Node.js functions, NOT Edge.** The README states "Instrument Node.js backends and scripts" and explicitly: "Edge runtime packaging ... is not supported." The exporter uses OTLP-proto + `protobufjs` + the Node OTel SDK, which is Node-runtime only. So set your Vercel route to the **Node.js runtime**, not Edge.
- **Strong inference (flag):** because export is **batched** (default `flushInterval: 5s`, `batchSize: 100`) and a serverless function freezes/suspends right after it returns the response, you must **`await flush()` (or `shutdown()`) before the handler returns**, or spans can be lost. This follows from the batching design in `src/core/client.ts` plus the setup guide's "flush before the script ends"; I did not find a Vercel-specific note in the repo, so treat the *necessity* as inferred-strong, not documented.

### 6. Thin wrapper module (emits to neatlogs when keyed, always records locally)

Dual-writes every step to an in-memory store (so your own UI renders the trace live, with or without a key) and, when `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` is set, also to neatlogs. neatlogs is loaded lazily so the module runs even if the package or key is absent.

```typescript
// lib/trace/priorproof-tracer.ts
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

export type StepKind =
  | 'WORKFLOW' | 'CHAIN' | 'AGENT' | 'TOOL'
  | 'RETRIEVER' | 'EMBEDDING' | 'GUARDRAIL' | 'MCP_TOOL';

export interface SpanRecord {
  id: string; parentId?: string; name: string; kind: StepKind;
  status: 'running' | 'ok' | 'error';
  input?: unknown; output?: unknown;
  error?: { message: string; stack?: string };
  attributes?: Record<string, unknown>;
  startedAt: number; endedAt?: number;
}
export interface TraceRecord {
  runId: string; workflow: string; neatlogs: boolean;
  startedAt: number; endedAt?: number; spans: SpanRecord[];
}
export interface StepHandle {
  readonly id: string;
  setOutput(v: unknown): void;
  setAttribute(k: string, v: unknown): void;
  fail(message: string, err?: unknown): void; // marks ERROR without aborting the run
}
export interface RunHandle {
  readonly runId: string;
  step<T>(o: { name: string; kind: StepKind; input?: unknown }, fn: (s: StepHandle) => T | Promise<T>): Promise<T>;
  setFinalOutput(v: unknown): void;
}
export interface Tracer {
  run<T>(o: { workflow: string; runId?: string; sessionId?: string }, fn: (r: RunHandle) => T | Promise<T>): Promise<T>;
  getTrace(runId: string): TraceRecord | undefined;
  listTraces(): TraceRecord[];
  subscribe(fn: (t: TraceRecord) => void): () => void; // live UI (SSE/poll)
  flush(): Promise<void>;    // call before a Vercel Node function returns
  shutdown(): Promise<void>; // call on process exit (CLI/long-lived)
}
```

```typescript
// lib/trace/priorproof-tracer.ts (continued)
type NL = typeof import('neatlogs');
let nlPromise: Promise<NL | null> | null = null;
async function loadNeatlogs(): Promise<NL | null> {
  if (!process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY) return null;        // graceful degradation: no key => local only
  if (!nlPromise) nlPromise = (async () => {
    try {
      const m = await import('neatlogs');                // lazy: module may be absent
      await m.init({ apiKey: process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY, workflowName: 'priorproof' });
      return m;
    } catch (e) { console.warn('[priorproof] neatlogs off, local-only trace:', e); return null; }
  })();
  return nlPromise;
}
const errOf = (e: unknown) => e instanceof Error ? { message: e.message, stack: e.stack } : { message: String(e) };

export function createTracer(): Tracer {
  const traces = new Map<string, TraceRecord>();
  const listeners = new Set<(t: TraceRecord) => void>();
  const parent = new AsyncLocalStorage<string | undefined>();
  const emit = (t: TraceRecord) => listeners.forEach(l => { try { l(t); } catch {} });

  return {
    getTrace: id => traces.get(id),
    listTraces: () => [...traces.values()],
    subscribe(fn) { listeners.add(fn); return () => listeners.delete(fn); },
    async flush() { const nl = await loadNeatlogs(); if (nl) await nl.flush(); },
    async shutdown() { const nl = await loadNeatlogs(); if (nl) await nl.shutdown(); },

    async run(o, fn) {
      const nl = await loadNeatlogs();
      const runId = o.runId ?? randomUUID();
      const t: TraceRecord = { runId, workflow: o.workflow, neatlogs: !!nl, startedAt: Date.now(), spans: [] };
      traces.set(runId, t); emit(t);

      const body = async (): Promise<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>>> => {
        const run: RunHandle = {
          runId,
          setFinalOutput(v) { if (nl) nl.setTraceOutput(v); },
          async step(so, sfn) {
            const rec: SpanRecord = {
              id: randomUUID(), parentId: parent.getStore(), name: so.name, kind: so.kind,
              status: 'running', input: so.input, startedAt: Date.now(),
            };
            t.spans.push(rec); emit(t);

            const exec = async (nlSpan?: { setStatus(s: { code: number; message?: string }): void; recordException(e: Error): void; setAttribute(k: string, v: unknown): void }) => {
              const h: StepHandle = {
                id: rec.id,
                setOutput: v => { rec.output = v; },
                setAttribute: (k, v) => { (rec.attributes ??= {})[k] = v; nlSpan?.setAttribute(k, typeof v === 'string' ? v : JSON.stringify(v)); },
                fail: (msg, err) => {
                  rec.status = 'error'; rec.error = err ? errOf(err) : { message: msg };
                  nlSpan?.setStatus({ code: 2 /* SpanStatusCode.ERROR */, message: msg });
                  nlSpan?.recordException(err instanceof Error ? err : new Error(msg));
                },
              };
              try {
                const out = await parent.run(rec.id, () => sfn(h));
                if (rec.output === undefined) rec.output = out;        // default output = return value
                if (rec.status === 'running') rec.status = 'ok';
                return out as Awaited<ReturnType<typeof sfn>>;
              } catch (e) {
                rec.status = 'error'; rec.error = errOf(e); throw e;    // rethrow => neatlogs marks ERROR too
              } finally { rec.endedAt = Date.now(); emit(t); }
            };

            // trace() (not span()) so a non-throwing fail() survives: span() forces OK on success.
            return nl
              ? await nl.trace({ name: so.name, kind: so.kind as any, input: so.input }, (sp: any) => exec(sp))
              : await exec();
          },
        };
        try { return await fn(run) as any; }
        finally { t.endedAt = Date.now(); emit(t); }
      };

      // Root WORKFLOW span wraps the whole run; children nest under it automatically.
      return nl
        ? await nl.trace({ name: o.workflow, kind: 'WORKFLOW' as any, sessionId: o.sessionId }, () => body())
        : await body();
    },
  };
}

export const tracer = createTracer();
```

**Example usage — the five PriorProof steps, with a refusal marked failed:**

```typescript
export async function runPriorAuth(request: PaRequest) {
  return tracer.run({ workflow: 'prior-auth', sessionId: request.caseId }, async (run) => {
    const criteria = await run.step({ name: 'policy-criterion-parse', kind: 'CHAIN', input: request.policyText },
      () => parseCriteria(request.policyText));

    const evidence = await run.step({ name: 'evidence-lookup', kind: 'RETRIEVER', input: request.patientId },
      () => fetchEvidence(request.patientId)); // throw inside => step auto-marked failed + run aborts

    const matches = await run.step({ name: 'evidence-match', kind: 'CHAIN', input: { criteria, evidence } },
      () => matchEvidence(criteria, evidence));

    const decision = await run.step({ name: 'criterion-decision', kind: 'AGENT', input: matches },
      (s) => { const d = decide(matches); s.setAttribute('priorproof.outcome', d.outcome); return d; });

    if (decision.outcome === 'refuse') {
      await run.step({ name: 'refusal', kind: 'GUARDRAIL', input: decision.reasons }, (s) => {
        s.fail(`Refused: ${decision.reasons.join('; ')}`); // marks ERROR, run continues (business refusal)
        return { refused: true, reasons: decision.reasons };
      });
    }
    run.setFinalOutput(decision);
    return decision;
  });
}
```

# PriorProof: cfo.ai usage note + business plan

## Part 1 — How cfo.ai is used for neatHack, and what it produces

neatHack is the neatlogs 48-hour AI-agent hackathon. The official rules state the stack plainly: "Your project must use neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai. Use neatlogs and Entire to build and improve your agent, and cfo.ai to plan its business." So cfo.ai is the mandatory business-planning layer, not a build tool. Its output goes in the submission as the business case for your agent. ([neatlogs.com/hackathon](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon))

## Part 2 — PriorProof business plan

### The US prior-authorization reality (every figure sourced)

These are the numbers the product sells against.

- **Volume.** A physician completes about **39 to 40 prior authorizations per week** (2024 AMA survey). Medicare Advantage alone ran **about 50 million prior-authorization determinations in 2023**, up from 46.2 million requests in 2022, and roughly 53 million in 2024. Commercial and Medicaid add much more on top. ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/about/leadership/latest-prior-auth-survey-shows-promised-reform-remains-elusive), [AHA on KFF 2023](https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2025-01-29-kff-ma-insurers-made-nearly-50-million-prior-authorization-determinations-2023), [KFF 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-plans-denied-a-larger-share-of-prior-authorization-requests-in-2022-than-in-prior-years/))
- **Time cost.** Prior auth consumes **about 13 hours of physician and staff time per practice per week**. **40% of practices employ staff who work only on prior authorizations**. That is roughly **20 minutes of clinician and staff time per request** (13 hours divided by about 39 requests). ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/about/leadership/latest-prior-auth-survey-shows-promised-reform-remains-elusive))
- **Dollar cost per request.** The 2023 CAQH Index puts a **manual prior authorization at about $10.91 to the provider**, versus about $2.17 fully electronic. CAQH CORE separately prices one manual prior auth at **$13.40 split across health plan and provider**. Loaded cost (rework, peer-to-peer, delays) runs higher in secondary estimates, in the $25 to $90 range. ([CAQH via Unlimited Systems](https://www.unlimitedsystems.com/blog/prior-auth-cost/), [CAQH CORE PA pilot brief](https://www.caqh.org/sites/default/files/core/white-paper/CORE_PA_Pilot_Issue_Brief_v7.pdf))
- **Denial rate.** MA insurers denied **7.4% of requests in 2022 and 6.4% in 2023** in whole or in part. ([KFF 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-plans-denied-a-larger-share-of-prior-authorization-requests-in-2022-than-in-prior-years/), [AHA on KFF 2023](https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2025-01-29-kff-ma-insurers-made-nearly-50-million-prior-authorization-determinations-2023))
- **Appeal rate.** Only **about 10 to 12% of denials are appealed** (9.9% in 2022, 11.7% in 2023). ([KFF 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-plans-denied-a-larger-share-of-prior-authorization-requests-in-2022-than-in-prior-years/), [AHA on KFF 2023](https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2025-01-29-kff-ma-insurers-made-nearly-50-million-prior-authorization-determinations-2023))
- **Overturn on appeal.** When providers do appeal, **over 80% of denials are overturned** (83.2% in 2022). The gap between a 6 to 7% denial rate, a 10% appeal rate and an 80%+ overturn rate is the core waste: most denials stand only because nobody fights them. ([KFF 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-plans-denied-a-larger-share-of-prior-authorization-requests-in-2022-than-in-prior-years/), [AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/over-80-prior-auth-appeals-succeed-why-aren-t-there-more))
- **Wrongful denials.** HHS OIG found **13% of MA prior-auth denials met Medicare coverage rules** and should have been approved, plus 18% of payment denials. ([HHS OIG OEI-09-18-00260](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2022/some-medicare-advantage-organization-denials-of-prior-authorization-requests-raise-concerns-about-beneficiary-access-to-medically-necessary-care/))
- **Cost of a denial.** Providers spend an average of **$43.84 to fight one denied claim**, about **$19.7 billion a year** in total denial-management expense. Reworking a single denied claim runs $25 and up. ([Premier](https://premierinc.com/newsroom/blog/trend-alert-private-payers-retain-profits-by-refusing-or-delaying-legitimate-medical-claims), [Becker's](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/finance/claims-denials-are-costing-hospitals-nearly-20b-per-year/))

### The buyer

PriorProof sells to whoever eats the prior-auth labor cost today.

- **Specialty practices** with high prior-auth load (oncology, cardiology, orthopedics, rheumatology, gastroenterology, radiology). These feel the 13-hours-a-week pain hardest and often staff a dedicated prior-auth person.
- **Revenue-cycle-management (RCM) firms** that run prior auth and denials for many practices. They buy volume and resell the time savings as margin.
- **Medical billing companies** that already hold the payer relationships and the charts.
- **Group practices and small hospital systems** with a central authorizations team.

The economic buyer is the practice administrator or the RCM operations lead. The budget already exists as salaried staff time, so this is a cost-substitution sale, not a net-new line item.

### Pricing

Three tiers. The flat per-packet price undercuts the loaded cost of a manual prior auth and sits near the narrow CAQH labor figure, so the ROI reads at a glance.

- **Pay as you go: $12 per completed packet.** No commitment. For small or occasional users. This is roughly half the low end of the loaded manual cost ($25 to $90) and about a quarter of the $43.84 it costs just to fight one denial.
- **Pro: $349 per seat per month**, includes 50 packets, then $7 per packet. For specialty practices and billing clerks with steady volume.
- **Scale: custom, $5 to $7 per packet** on an annual commit, with BAA, SSO and audit logs. For RCM and billing companies.

Across the mix the **blended realized price is about $9 per packet**. The defensible anchor: even the narrow CAQH labor cost is about $11 per manual prior auth, and the loaded cost is $25 to $90, so a $9 to $12 finished packet saves the buyer money on the direct-labor basis alone and much more once rework and denials are counted.

### COGS

Variable cost is dominated by LLM spend. The flow is: parse the policy into criteria, locate candidate chart spans per criterion, prove or refuse each criterion against a cited span, then assemble the packet.

Per-packet model assumptions:
- About **10 criteria per policy**, a few calls each (locate, prove, format), plus about 5 assembly calls. Call it **~35 model calls per packet**.
- Shared context (policy plus relevant chart, about 23k tokens) is cached once and read cheaply on later calls. Prompt caching reads at about 0.1x the input rate, which is what makes this viable.
- Per packet that works out to roughly **300k cached-read input tokens, 35k fresh input tokens and 20k output tokens**.

On a mid-tier frontier model as the reference (Claude Sonnet 5 list price $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output, cache reads at 0.1x), the arithmetic is about **$0.48 per packet**. Rounding up for retries, longer charts and a QA pass gives a planning number of **about $0.60 per packet**. A cheaper model for the extraction subcalls (Haiku-class at $1 / $5 per million) pulls it toward $0.20. A top-tier model throughout (Opus-class at $5 / $25) pushes it to about $1.20. ([Anthropic pricing](https://www.anthropic.com/pricing))

- **Hosting on Vercel: roughly $20 to $150 per month**, mostly fixed. Vercel Pro starts at about $20 per member per month plus usage. Serverless function compute per packet is a few cents.
- **Other fixed infra:** a Postgres database (Neon or Vercel Postgres), error monitoring, domain and email. Call it **$150 to $300 per month all-in for a solo founder** including Vercel.
- **Payment processing:** about 3% on card revenue, folded into the tier economics.

Planning figure: **variable cost ~$0.60 per packet**, fixed infra **~$200 per month**.

### Gross margin and unit economics

- Blended price per packet: **$9.00**
- Variable cost per packet: **$0.60**
- **Contribution per packet: $8.40**
- **Gross margin: about 93%**

This is standard AI-application economics. The product is labor it replaces at near-zero marginal cost.

### Break-even

- **Infra-only break-even: about 25 packets per month** ($200 fixed divided by $8.40 contribution). This is trivially cleared by a single pilot.
- **Break-even including a $3,000 per month founder draw: about 380 packets per month** ($3,200 divided by $8.40).

For scale: one five-physician specialty group generates about **840 prior authorizations per month** (39 per physician per week times 5, times 4.33 weeks). So a single mid-size group, even at partial adoption, covers the founder's salary and the infra several times over.

Central assumption is the packet ramp, gated by the healthcare sales cycle and BAA onboarding. Blended price $9, variable cost $0.60, fixed plus founder draw $3,200 per month, starting cash $15,000.

### The value anchor

What the buyer gets per packet, in the real figures:

- **Time reclaimed: about 20 minutes of clinician and staff time per request** (13 hours per week over about 39 requests). PriorProof returns a finished, cited packet, so it gives back most of that 20 minutes.
- **Direct cost undercut:** a manual prior auth costs the provider about **$11** in CAQH labor terms and **$25 to $90 loaded**. A $9 to $12 packet is cheaper than the keystrokes on the narrow number and a fraction of the loaded cost.
- **Denials avoided:** 6 to 7% of MA requests are denied, and a large share of those are missing-documentation denials. A criterion-complete, span-cited submission attacks exactly that class. When a denial still lands, over 80% of appeals win, yet only about 10% get appealed because appeals cost $43.84 each to fight. PriorProof's cited spans and named gaps make both the first submission and any appeal cheap to produce, which is where the recoverable money sits.
- **Wrongful-denial recovery:** HHS OIG found 13% of MA denials were actually wrong. An evidence-complete packet is the lever that turns those into overturns instead of write-offs.

The one-line pitch: **PriorProof turns 20 minutes of clinician time and an $11 to $90 manual task into a $9 cited packet, and it makes the 80% of appeals that win cheap enough to actually file.**

PriorProof handles PHI, so HIPAA applies and a signed BAA is required with every subprocessor that touches charts: the hosting provider and the LLM vendor. 2. *"Member has signs or symptoms of neural compression (radiculopathy, neurogenic extremity claudication, myelopathy) associated with the levels being treated; and"*

<result>Research complete. I read the neatHack page plus the Entire docs (quickstart, installation, checkpoints capture/inspect, Graph setup, Brain overview/quickstart, glossary, CLI reference index, and the CLI repo README). Below is the deliverable, with confirmed-vs-inferred separated and a human-handoff checklist at the end.

Note on method: the WebFetch helper model repeatedly appended "I'm not a Claude agent" meta-commentary. That is an artifact of the summarizer reacting to the task framing, not anything in Entire's docs. I ignored it. The technical extractions themselves are sound and I cross-checked the load-bearing facts across multiple pages.

---

## Sources

- neatHack / Entire hackathon page: https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/
- Entire product site: https://entire.io/
- Docs quickstart: https://docs.entire.io/quickstart
- Docs installation + CLI README: https://docs.entire.io/installation.md and https://github.com/entireio/cli
- Capture checkpoints: https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/capture-checkpoints
- Inspect checkpoints (web): https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-in-entire-io.md
- Inspect checkpoints (CLI): https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-in-cli.md
- Graph setup: https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/set-up-graph.md
- Brain overview + quickstart: https://docs.entire.io/guides/brain/overview.md and /quickstart.md
- Glossary: https://docs.entire.io/glossary.md
- Full doc index: https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt

---

## 1. Install the CLI (confirmed from docs)

Linux (your platform) and the general-purpose path:
```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
# nightly channel: curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly
entire version   # verify
```

macOS alternative (Homebrew 6.0.10+):
```bash
brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire
```

From Go source (needs Go 1.27.1+, this is the only path that needs Go; packaged installs bundle their own runtime):
```bash
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/git-remote-entire@latest
export PATH="$HOME/go/bin:$PATH"
```

The CLI is MIT-licensed and open source (repo github.com/entireio/cli).

Prerequisites (confirmed): Git installed and configured; a GitHub account with an accessible repo; an AI coding agent installed (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.); macOS/Linux/Windows. Optional: the `gh` CLI if you want to create a demo repo from the terminal. A C compiler is NOT required for the standard prebuilt installs; the hackathon page mentions a C compiler only for building Brain/Graph tree-sitter bindings from source, which you avoid by using the prebuilt installers.

Important mechanism (confirmed): Entire works by installing git hooks plus agent hooks in your repo. It captures your AI coding-agent SESSION and links it to a git COMMIT. That pairing is a checkpoint. This is a development-time tool that records how the code was built; it is not a runtime state store for your own deployed agent (this matters for your PriorProof design, see section 5).

---

## 2. Authenticate and connect GitHub

### Interactive vs headless (confirmed from the CLI README)

Login command: `entire login`.
- Default: opens a browser, sign in with GitHub, tokens stored in the OS keyring. This is the OAuth/browser step and must be done by the human.
- Headless box with a browser elsewhere: `entire login --device` forces a device-code flow (it also falls back to this automatically when no local browser). A human still has to open the shown URL and enter the code once.
- File-backed token storage instead of keyring: `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file entire login` writes `tokens.json` at mode 0600 (path overridable via `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`).
- Fully non-interactive / CI: `ENTIRE_TOKEN=<JWT> entire ...` injects a login-or-service-account session token per invocation, bypasses stored creds, writes nothing to disk. `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` exists for checkpoint-repo git operations.
- Account management: `entire auth status`, `entire auth switch`, `entire auth token`; `entire logout`.

### GitHub App + repo connection (confirmed)

Two separate things authenticate you: (1) `entire login` for the CLI, and (2) the Entire GitHub App, which must be installed and granted access to the repo. Nothing repo-related shows on entire.io until the GitHub App is installed and the repo imported. Access then mirrors the GitHub collaborator list (no separate invites). Sync "can take up to an hour."

CLI mirror flow (connect an existing GitHub repo to Entire's network):
```bash
entire login
entire repo mirror add
entire repo remote add entire      # adds an 'entire' git remote
git remote -v
git fetch entire
git push entire
# optional, repoint origin at the mirror:
# entire repo remote add origin --override
```

What is scriptable headlessly: install, `entire enable -y`, mirror add, remote add, all git push/commit, `entire checkpoint ...`, Graph and Brain install/setup. CI auth via `ENTIRE_TOKEN`.
What needs a human with a browser (once): the first `entire login` (or the device-code entry) and authorizing the Entire GitHub App on the `zkasuran` account and granting it the `priorproof` repo. Org-owned repos need an org admin to approve the app.

---

## 3. Capture a checkpoint, and get the link + ID for the submission

### Capture (confirmed)

```bash
entire enable -y --agent claude-code     # once per repo; installs hooks
# ...run your coding agent, make a focused change...
git add path/to/changed-file
git commit -m "Add chart extraction stage"
# Entire prompts at commit time: "Link this commit to session context? [Y]es/[n]o/[a]lways"
```
Press `y` (or `a` for always). To preset it and skip the prompt, add to `.entire/settings.local.json` (personal) or `.entire/settings.json` (team):
```json
{ "commit_linking": "always" }
```
A valid checkpoint requires BOTH captured session context AND a git commit. One session can produce several checkpoints (one per commit); one checkpoint can span several sessions.

Inspect (confirmed):
```bash
entire checkpoint list                       # prints checkpoint IDs; --json, --session ID
entire checkpoint explain HEAD               # explain by commit-ish...
entire checkpoint explain <CHECKPOINT_ID>    # ...or by ULID / unambiguous prefix
entire checkpoint explain <ID> --generate    # AI summary (needs a provider CLI logged in)
entire checkpoint search "coverage logic"    # find a checkpoint by text/meaning
entire checkpoint tokens <ID> --compare <BASELINE_ID>
```

### The accessible link + ID (confirmed)

- Checkpoint ID: a 26-char ULID that lands in the commit message as a trailer, verbatim example from the docs:
  ```
  Entire-Checkpoint: 01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN
  ```
  Read it with `entire checkpoint list` or by inspecting the commit trailer.
- Shareable web link (exact format from the docs):
  ```
  https://entire.io/gh/<org>/<repo>/commit/<full-commit-sha>
  ```
  For you: `https://entire.io/gh/zkasuran/priorproof/commit/<SHA>`. The page shows Sessions (prompt, transcript, tool calls) and Changes (diffs) tabs.

For the neatHack submission, give both: the entire.io commit URL and the `Entire-Checkpoint:` ULID.

Access caveat (partly inferred): the link resolves only after the repo is mirrored/imported to entire.io via the GitHub App, and after you push. The hackathon page states the URL alone grants nothing and that checkpoints in public repos are public; the core docs say mirror access follows GitHub collaborator permissions but do not spell out anonymous-viewer rules. Safest path to a judge-accessible link: make `zkasuran/priorproof` public, mirror it, push, then `entire status` to confirm sync before pasting the link. Confirm with a signed-out browser that the link opens.

---

## 4. Trails, Graph, Brain

Prize scope (confirmed from the hackathon page): "Best Use of Entire" rewards the most creative use of Checkpoints, Graph, or Brain. Trails is not named in the prize criteria, so treat it as optional polish, not a scored feature.

### Checkpoints
Covered above. Glossary: "A save point for your work. Entire creates checkpoints around agent activity and links committed ones to Git commits."

### Graph (confirmed, except where noted)
`entire-graph` is a plugin that maps your repo's code and relationships so an agent can locate implementations and trace what calls what. Prereqs: Entire CLI 0.10.0+, Git 2.36+, a local git repo, and an agent that reads `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`.
```bash
entire plugin install graph
entire graph version
entire graph init-agents --repo .   # writes .entire/graph-agent.md, updates AGENTS.md & CLAUDE.md
git add .entire/graph-agent.md AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Enable entire-graph"
```
Inferred / unconfirmed: the hackathon page's `entire graph stats --repo .` and the "save up to 71% token spend" figure appear on the hackathon/marketing pages but NOT on the Graph setup doc, so do not state them as settled. Do not hand-edit `.entire/graph-agent.md` (regenerated on rerun).

### Brain (confirmed)
Glossary has no entry, but the overview defines it as shared, repo-resident agent memory: find earlier decisions, save lessons, hand context to an agent before it starts. It carries context across agents (start in Claude Code, continue in Codex). Prereqs: a local git repo with at least one commit, the Entire CLI, Git 2.36+ (no Go/C-compiler needed).
```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
entire plugin install graph           # optional, enables code-index-backed inspection
entire brain setup                    # add --no-backfill --no-daemon to avoid auto fact-extraction + background watcher
entire brain status
entire brain init-agents              # writes .entire/agent-guide.md, references it in AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md
entire brain mcp --print-config
claude mcp add entire-brain -- entire brain mcp   # register Brain as an MCP server for Claude Code
```
Usage commands (confirmed): `entire brain overview`, `entire brain brief "<task>"`, `entire brain query [--keyword|--semantic] "<q>"`, `entire brain remember "<fact>" --path a.b.c`, `entire brain recall "<topic>"`, `entire brain inspect impact <Symbol>` and `inspect changes` (need Graph), `entire brain status --verbose`, `entire brain verify`.
Cost warning (confirmed): default `entire brain setup` extracts facts from past sessions and runs a background watcher, which can send session content to a model provider and incur token charges. Use `--no-backfill --no-daemon` to avoid that.

### Trails (confirmed definition, commands partly unconfirmed)
Glossary: a Trail is "Entire's unit of work, covering one branch and one pull request from one intent to shipped code." A Runner is "a config-driven job that runs an AI coding agent in an isolated cloud sandbox against a branch or trail." So Trails = automated per-push CI/agent-review on a branch backed by a GitHub PR.
Feature-flagged (inferred): the hackathon page says you request access via a form, then in entire.io Settings → General enable Runners, Auto build on push, and Trails, then run `entire runner setup -y` and `entire trail create`. `entire runner` is in the stable CLI reference; `entire trail create` is NOT in the published CLI reference index, so treat that exact command as unconfirmed/experimental. For a solo 48h build, Trails is skippable.

---

## 5. Using checkpoints meaningfully in PriorProof (important correction)

Your example "checkpoint the parsed chart after extraction and the coverage state before packet assembly, so a run resumes without re-reading the chart" describes runtime state-snapshotting of the deployed prior-auth agent. Entire does not do that. Entire checkpoints are development-time pairings of a coding-agent session with a git commit. It will not natively snapshot your Next.js app's execution state on Vercel. State that plainly in planning so the submission narrative stays honest.

Two clean ways to make the idea real and still win "Best Use of Entire":

- Map each pipeline stage to its own checkpoint during the build. Build chart-extraction, coverage-lookup, and packet-assembly each in a dedicated agent session and commit each as its own checkpoint with a descriptive message. A judge then runs `entire checkpoint explain <ID>` or opens the commit URL and sees the reasoning, prompts, and diffs behind each stage. This is the most direct, confirmed, meaningful use, and it is exactly what the checkpoint link in the submission should showcase. Pair it with Graph (so the agent navigates the growing codebase cheaply) and Brain (persist decisions like "coverage rules live in X, prove-or-refuse threshold is Y" via `entire brain remember`, recalled in later sessions). Using all three is the strongest claim for the prize.
- Implement the runtime resume as a PriorProof app feature in its own right (write parsed-chart JSON and coverage state to disk or a store, resume from there), which is good engineering independent of Entire. If you want an Entire angle on the actual agent run, Entire's confirmed resume primitive is cross-session, not cross-request: `entire session resume` / Resume Sessions continues a stopped coding session or hands work between agents. Tell the "resume without re-reading the chart" story as your app feature; do not attribute it to Entire checkpoints.

Submission pointer (confirmed): neatHack requires an accessible checkpoint link + ID. Use the checkpoint for your most illustrative stage commit (for example the coverage/packet-assembly commit), give its entire.io/gh/... URL and its `Entire-Checkpoint:` ULID.

---

## 6. Exact command sequence for a solo builder (start to finish)

```bash
# 0. One-time: human does browser auth (see checklist) ---------------------
entire login                 # browser OAuth; or: entire login --device

# 1. Install ---------------------------------------------------------------
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
entire version

# 2. Enable Entire in the repo --------------------------------------------
cd ~/path/to/priorproof
entire enable -y --agent claude-code
entire status

# 3. Preset commit linking so builds don't block on a prompt --------------
mkdir -p .entire
printf '{ "commit_linking": "always" }\n' > .entire/settings.local.json

# 4. (Recommended for the prize) Graph + Brain ----------------------------
entire plugin install graph
entire graph init-agents --repo .
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
entire brain setup --no-backfill --no-daemon
entire brain init-agents
claude mcp add entire-brain -- entire brain mcp
git add .entire/graph-agent.md .entire/agent-guide.md AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Enable Entire graph and brain"

# 5. Build in stages; each stage = one checkpoint -------------------------
#   run your coding agent for the chart-extraction stage, then:
git add src/extract/
git commit -m "Add chart extraction stage"
#   repeat for coverage lookup, packet assembly, each its own commit

# 6. Connect GitHub mirror + push so the web link resolves ----------------
entire repo mirror add
entire repo remote add entire
git push -u origin HEAD        # push to GitHub
git push entire                # push to the Entire mirror
entire status                  # confirm sync

# 7. Grab the submission link + ID ----------------------------------------
entire checkpoint list                 # note the ULID of the stage you want to showcase
entire checkpoint explain <CHECKPOINT_ID>
#   Link:  https://entire.io/gh/zkasuran/priorproof/commit/<FULL_SHA>
#   ID:    01K...   (the Entire-Checkpoint ULID)

# 8. Verify the link opens signed-out, then paste both into the neatHack submission
```

---

## 7. Human handoff checklist (the browser/OAuth steps)

These cannot be scripted headlessly and need a human with a browser:

1. Run `entire login`, complete GitHub sign-in and consent in the browser (or `entire login --device` and enter the code at the shown URL).
2. Install/authorize the Entire GitHub App on the `zkasuran` account and grant it access to the `priorproof` repo. If the repo is org-owned, an org admin must approve the app. Allow up to an hour for sync.
3. Make `zkasuran/priorproof` public (or confirm judges have collaborator access) so the entire.io checkpoint link is openable by graders. Verify by opening the link in a signed-out browser.
4. Trails only (optional, skip for a solo 48h build): submit the Trails access-request form, then in entire.io Settings → General toggle Runners, Auto build on push, and Trails.
5. For `entire checkpoint explain --generate` AI summaries or Brain's model-backed features: the underlying provider CLI must be logged in (one-time, interactive).

Everything else (install, enable, mirror, commits, pushes, checkpoint list/explain, Graph/Brain install and setup, CI via `ENTIRE_TOKEN`) is scriptable without a human.

---

## 8. Confirmed vs inferred, at a glance

Confirmed from docs: all install commands and MIT license; prerequisites; `entire login` browser-default plus `--device`, `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file`, `ENTIRE_TOKEN` CI flow, `entire auth`; GitHub App requirement and collaborator-based access; mirror commands; `entire enable --agent`, agent list, commit-link prompt and `commit_linking:always`; checkpoint = session + commit; `entire checkpoint list/explain/search/tokens`; ULID checkpoint ID in the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer; share URL `https://entire.io/gh/<org>/<repo>/commit/<sha>`; Graph install/version/init-agents and its prereqs; Brain install (get-brain.sh), setup/status/init-agents/mcp, the full usage command set, and the token-cost warning; Trail and Runner glossary definitions; the "Best Use of Entire" prize covering Checkpoints/Graph/Brain.

Inferred or unconfirmed (flagged, do not state as settled): `entire graph stats` and the "71% token saving" figure (hackathon/marketing pages only); `entire trail create` as an exact command and the Trails enablement flow (hackathon page only, Trails is feature-flagged and `trail` is absent from the stable CLI reference); exact anonymous-viewer access rules for the share link (docs give collaborator-based access; hackathon page says public-repo checkpoints are public). The whole "runtime resume via checkpoints" premise is a mismatch with what Entire does and I corrected it in section 5.

Could not fully confirm: whether a mirrored commit link is viewable with zero authentication for a public repo (strongly implied by the hackathon page, not spelled out in core docs). Test it signed-out before submitting.</result>

## PriorProof × neatlogs: TypeScript/Node instrumentation

### 1. Package name and version (CONFIRMED)

- npm package: **`neatlogs`** (unscoped). Current version **1.1.28**, license MIT, `engines.node >=18.0.0`.
- Source repo: **github.com/neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript** (the npm `neatlogs` package IS this TS SDK; the Python SDK is a separate `neatlogs` on PyPI).
- It is **OpenTelemetry-native** (depends on `@opentelemetry/*` and `protobufjs`); it exports OTLP-proto spans over HTTP.
- Related package: `@neatlogs/wizard` (v0.1.11), the `npx @neatlogs/wizard` auto-setup CLI. Not needed if you instrument by hand.

```bash
npm install neatlogs
```

Sources: [neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript README](https://github.com/neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript) · npm registry `registry.npmjs.org/neatlogs` (dist-tags.latest = 1.1.28) · [hackathon setup guide](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/neatlogs-setup-guide.html).

### 2. Initialization (CONFIRMED)

- Env var: **`NEATLOGS_API_KEY`**. There is **no project id for the SDK** — the API key itself selects the project.
- Two keys exist in the dashboard and they are not interchangeable: use the **Project API key** (the top one) for the Node SDK. The **HTTP ingest key starting with `nlw_`** is for raw HTTP / the browser SDK only; passing `nlw_` to the Node SDK returns 401. (`NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` + `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` exist only for reading traces back via the CLI/public API, not for ingest.)

```typescript
import { init, shutdown, wrapOpenAI } from 'neatlogs';
import OpenAI from 'openai';

await init({ apiKey: process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY, workflowName: 'my-first-app' });
const client = wrapOpenAI(new OpenAI());
// ...
await shutdown(); // flushes anything still queued
```

Key `init()` options (from the README `InitOptions` table): `apiKey` (default `process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY`, export disabled if unset), `workflowName`, `userId`, `tags`, `metadata`, `debug`, `disableExport`, `sampleRate`, `captureLogs` (needed for `log()`), `endpoint` (default `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`; SDK posts to `/v1/traces` and `/v1/logs`), `registerShutdownHandlers` (default true). Ingest uses header `x-api-key` + gzip (confirmed in `src/core/client.ts`). Must be wrapped in an `async function main()`; no top-level await.

### 3. Trace for one run + spans per step (CONFIRMED)

**`init()` does not monkeypatch.** You get spans two ways, and you can mix them:

- `span(options, fn)` — higher-order wrapper; returns an instrumented version of `fn` that auto-captures input, output, timing, errors. `kind` is required.
- `trace(options, fn)` — inline; runs the callback immediately, passes it the live OTel span, auto-captures `options.input` and the callback's return value, and creates a root trace when `sessionId` is set. Nesting is automatic: a `span()`/`trace()` called inside another becomes its child via OTel context.

`SpanKind` values (for `span()`): `WORKFLOW, AGENT, CHAIN, TOOL, RETRIEVER, EMBEDDING, MCP_TOOL, GUARDRAIL`. `trace()` additionally accepts `LLM, RERANKER, VECTOR_STORE` plus `GUARDRAIL, EVALUATOR`.

Mapping for PriorProof's five steps: policy criterion parse → `CHAIN`; evidence lookup → `RETRIEVER` (or `TOOL`); evidence match → `CHAIN`; criterion decision → `AGENT` or `CHAIN`; refusal → `GUARDRAIL`. One agent run = one `WORKFLOW` root.

Inputs/outputs attach automatically (`captureInput`/`captureOutput` default `true` on `span()`; `trace()` captures `input` and the returned value). Extra data: `setAttribute()` on the span, `log('msg {x}', { x })` for timestamped steps (requires `captureLogs: true`), and `setTraceOutput(value)` to override the trace's displayed final output (stamped as `neatlogs.trace.output` on the root).

**Marking a step failed (CONFIRMED, with an important nuance):**
- The built-in mechanism is to **throw** inside the wrapped fn/callback. The SDK catches it, calls `span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR, message })` and `span.recordException(err)`, then rethrows (`src/core/context.ts` lines 457-465; `src/decorators/base.ts` lines 291-297).
- Nuance that matters for a prove-or-refuse agent: **`span()` forces `setStatus(OK)` on success** (`base.ts:242`), so it will overwrite a manual error status if the fn returns normally. **`trace()` does not reset status on success**, so to mark a step failed *without aborting the run* (e.g. a refusal that is a business outcome, not a crash) you must use `trace()` and call `span.setStatus({ code: 2 /* ERROR */ })` + `span.recordException(...)` on the span the callback receives, then return normally. My wrapper below uses `trace()` for exactly this reason.

### 4. Shareable dashboard link (PARTIALLY CONFIRMED — flag)

- Traces land in the dashboard at **`https://app.neatlogs.com`** (EU: `https://eu.app.neatlogs.com`), inside the project, under the **Traces** tab; a row appears within a few seconds and expands to show the workflow tree, each step, tokens, and output. Confirmed in the setup guide and `src/trace-cli.ts` (`DEFAULT_HOST`, `NEATLOGS_HOST`).
- Programmatic read-back: `GET /api/v1/public/traces/<traceId>` on the app host, authenticated with `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` (service-account token, scope `observability:read`) + `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` (`src/trace-cli.ts:101`, `:28-29`). Internal/doctor path is `/api/traces/v3/<traceId>`.
- **Could not confirm from primary sources:** a tokenless *public* share-URL generator. The SDK exposes **no** function that mints a shareable link, and I found no in-app trace-URL path in the source beyond the authenticated API routes above. So a submission that "points at the dashboard" either (a) links the `app.neatlogs.com` project/trace page, which judges may need project access to view, or (b) is better served by PriorProof rendering its own trace from the local store (section 6) and/or reading back via the authenticated public API. **Flag this to the team**: verify in the live dashboard whether there is a "Share" button that produces a public link, since that is a UI feature the SDK does not surface.

### 5. LLM wrapper vs manual, and Vercel (CONFIRMED + one strong inference)

- **Both.** Explicit LLM-client wrappers exist and are **not** auto-instrumentation — you call them yourself: `wrapOpenAI`, `wrapAnthropic`, `wrapAzureOpenAI`, `wrapBedrock`, `wrapGoogleGenAI`/`wrapVertexAI`, `wrapAISDK` (Vercel AI SDK, import `neatlogs/ai`), plus framework hooks (`langchainHandler()`, `openaiAgentsProcessor()`, `wrapMastra`, `wrapClaudeAgentSDK`, etc.). Manual spans via `span()`/`trace()` cover everything that is not an LLM call (your evidence lookup, matching, decision logic). For PriorProof you will mostly want manual spans for the deterministic steps and a wrapper around whichever LLM client parses criteria.
- **Server-side on Vercel: works in Node.js functions, NOT Edge.** The README states "Instrument Node.js backends and scripts" and explicitly: "Edge runtime packaging ... is not supported." The exporter uses OTLP-proto + `protobufjs` + the Node OTel SDK, which is Node-runtime only. So set your Vercel route to the **Node.js runtime**, not Edge.
- **Strong inference (flag):** because export is **batched** (default `flushInterval: 5s`, `batchSize: 100`) and a serverless function freezes/suspends right after it returns the response, you must **`await flush()` (or `shutdown()`) before the handler returns**, or spans can be lost. This follows from the batching design in `src/core/client.ts` plus the setup guide's "flush before the script ends"; I did not find a Vercel-specific note in the repo, so treat the *necessity* as inferred-strong, not documented.

### 6. Thin wrapper module (emits to neatlogs when keyed, always records locally)

Dual-writes every step to an in-memory store (so your own UI renders the trace live, with or without a key) and, when `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` is set, also to neatlogs. neatlogs is loaded lazily so the module runs even if the package or key is absent.

```typescript
// lib/trace/priorproof-tracer.ts
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

export type StepKind =
  | 'WORKFLOW' | 'CHAIN' | 'AGENT' | 'TOOL'
  | 'RETRIEVER' | 'EMBEDDING' | 'GUARDRAIL' | 'MCP_TOOL';

export interface SpanRecord {
  id: string; parentId?: string; name: string; kind: StepKind;
  status: 'running' | 'ok' | 'error';
  input?: unknown; output?: unknown;
  error?: { message: string; stack?: string };
  attributes?: Record<string, unknown>;
  startedAt: number; endedAt?: number;
}
export interface TraceRecord {
  runId: string; workflow: string; neatlogs: boolean;
  startedAt: number; endedAt?: number; spans: SpanRecord[];
}
export interface StepHandle {
  readonly id: string;
  setOutput(v: unknown): void;
  setAttribute(k: string, v: unknown): void;
  fail(message: string, err?: unknown): void; // marks ERROR without aborting the run
}
export interface RunHandle {
  readonly runId: string;
  step<T>(o: { name: string; kind: StepKind; input?: unknown }, fn: (s: StepHandle) => T | Promise<T>): Promise<T>;
  setFinalOutput(v: unknown): void;
}
export interface Tracer {
  run<T>(o: { workflow: string; runId?: string; sessionId?: string }, fn: (r: RunHandle) => T | Promise<T>): Promise<T>;
  getTrace(runId: string): TraceRecord | undefined;
  listTraces(): TraceRecord[];
  subscribe(fn: (t: TraceRecord) => void): () => void; // live UI (SSE/poll)
  flush(): Promise<void>;    // call before a Vercel Node function returns
  shutdown(): Promise<void>; // call on process exit (CLI/long-lived)
}
```

```typescript
// lib/trace/priorproof-tracer.ts (continued)
type NL = typeof import('neatlogs');
let nlPromise: Promise<NL | null> | null = null;
async function loadNeatlogs(): Promise<NL | null> {
  if (!process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY) return null;        // graceful degradation: no key => local only
  if (!nlPromise) nlPromise = (async () => {
    try {
      const m = await import('neatlogs');                // lazy: module may be absent
      await m.init({ apiKey: process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY, workflowName: 'priorproof' });
      return m;
    } catch (e) { console.warn('[priorproof] neatlogs off, local-only trace:', e); return null; }
  })();
  return nlPromise;
}
const errOf = (e: unknown) => e instanceof Error ? { message: e.message, stack: e.stack } : { message: String(e) };

export function createTracer(): Tracer {
  const traces = new Map<string, TraceRecord>();
  const listeners = new Set<(t: TraceRecord) => void>();
  const parent = new AsyncLocalStorage<string | undefined>();
  const emit = (t: TraceRecord) => listeners.forEach(l => { try { l(t); } catch {} });

  return {
    getTrace: id => traces.get(id),
    listTraces: () => [...traces.values()],
    subscribe(fn) { listeners.add(fn); return () => listeners.delete(fn); },
    async flush() { const nl = await loadNeatlogs(); if (nl) await nl.flush(); },
    async shutdown() { const nl = await loadNeatlogs(); if (nl) await nl.shutdown(); },

    async run(o, fn) {
      const nl = await loadNeatlogs();
      const runId = o.runId ?? randomUUID();
      const t: TraceRecord = { runId, workflow: o.workflow, neatlogs: !!nl, startedAt: Date.now(), spans: [] };
      traces.set(runId, t); emit(t);

      const body = async (): Promise<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>>> => {
        const run: RunHandle = {
          runId,
          setFinalOutput(v) { if (nl) nl.setTraceOutput(v); },
          async step(so, sfn) {
            const rec: SpanRecord = {
              id: randomUUID(), parentId: parent.getStore(), name: so.name, kind: so.kind,
              status: 'running', input: so.input, startedAt: Date.now(),
            };
            t.spans.push(rec); emit(t);

            const exec = async (nlSpan?: { setStatus(s: { code: number; message?: string }): void; recordException(e: Error): void; setAttribute(k: string, v: unknown): void }) => {
              const h: StepHandle = {
                id: rec.id,
                setOutput: v => { rec.output = v; },
                setAttribute: (k, v) => { (rec.attributes ??= {})[k] = v; nlSpan?.setAttribute(k, typeof v === 'string' ? v : JSON.stringify(v)); },
                fail: (msg, err) => {
                  rec.status = 'error'; rec.error = err ? errOf(err) : { message: msg };
                  nlSpan?.setStatus({ code: 2 /* SpanStatusCode.ERROR */, message: msg });
                  nlSpan?.recordException(err instanceof Error ? err : new Error(msg));
                },
              };
              try {
                const out = await parent.run(rec.id, () => sfn(h));
                if (rec.output === undefined) rec.output = out;        // default output = return value
                if (rec.status === 'running') rec.status = 'ok';
                return out as Awaited<ReturnType<typeof sfn>>;
              } catch (e) {
                rec.status = 'error'; rec.error = errOf(e); throw e;    // rethrow => neatlogs marks ERROR too
              } finally { rec.endedAt = Date.now(); emit(t); }
            };

            // trace() (not span()) so a non-throwing fail() survives: span() forces OK on success.
            return nl
              ? await nl.trace({ name: so.name, kind: so.kind as any, input: so.input }, (sp: any) => exec(sp))
              : await exec();
          },
        };
        try { return await fn(run) as any; }
        finally { t.endedAt = Date.now(); emit(t); }
      };

      // Root WORKFLOW span wraps the whole run; children nest under it automatically.
      return nl
        ? await nl.trace({ name: o.workflow, kind: 'WORKFLOW' as any, sessionId: o.sessionId }, () => body())
        : await body();
    },
  };
}

export const tracer = createTracer();
```

**Example usage — the five PriorProof steps, with a refusal marked failed:**

```typescript
export async function runPriorAuth(request: PaRequest) {
  return tracer.run({ workflow: 'prior-auth', sessionId: request.caseId }, async (run) => {
    const criteria = await run.step({ name: 'policy-criterion-parse', kind: 'CHAIN', input: request.policyText },
      () => parseCriteria(request.policyText));

    const evidence = await run.step({ name: 'evidence-lookup', kind: 'RETRIEVER', input: request.patientId },
      () => fetchEvidence(request.patientId)); // throw inside => step auto-marked failed + run aborts

    const matches = await run.step({ name: 'evidence-match', kind: 'CHAIN', input: { criteria, evidence } },
      () => matchEvidence(criteria, evidence));

    const decision = await run.step({ name: 'criterion-decision', kind: 'AGENT', input: matches },
      (s) => { const d = decide(matches); s.setAttribute('priorproof.outcome', d.outcome); return d; });

    if (decision.outcome === 'refuse') {
      await run.step({ name: 'refusal', kind: 'GUARDRAIL', input: decision.reasons }, (s) => {
        s.fail(`Refused: ${decision.reasons.join('; ')}`); // marks ERROR, run continues (business refusal)
        return { refused: true, reasons: decision.reasons };
      });
    }
    run.setFinalOutput(decision);
    return decision;
  });
}
```

## Part 2 — PriorProof business plan

### The US prior-authorization reality (every figure sourced)

These are the numbers the product sells against.

- **Volume.** A physician completes about **39 to 40 prior authorizations per week** (2024 AMA survey). Medicare Advantage alone ran **about 50 million prior-authorization determinations in 2023**, up from 46.2 million requests in 2022, and roughly 53 million in 2024. Commercial and Medicaid add much more on top. ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/about/leadership/latest-prior-auth-survey-shows-promised-reform-remains-elusive), [AHA on KFF 2023](https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2025-01-29-kff-ma-insurers-made-nearly-50-million-prior-authorization-determinations-2023), [KFF 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-plans-denied-a-larger-share-of-prior-authorization-requests-in-2022-than-in-prior-years/))
- **Time cost.** Prior auth consumes **about 13 hours of physician and staff time per practice per week**. **40% of practices employ staff who work only on prior authorizations**. That is roughly **20 minutes of clinician and staff time per request** (13 hours divided by about 39 requests). ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/about/leadership/latest-prior-auth-survey-shows-promised-reform-remains-elusive))
- **Dollar cost per request.** The 2023 CAQH Index puts a **manual prior authorization at about $10.91 to the provider**, versus about $2.17 fully electronic. CAQH CORE separately prices one manual prior auth at **$13.40 split across health plan and provider**. Loaded cost (rework, peer-to-peer, delays) runs higher in secondary estimates, in the $25 to $90 range. ([CAQH via Unlimited Systems](https://www.unlimitedsystems.com/blog/prior-auth-cost/), [CAQH CORE PA pilot brief](https://www.caqh.org/sites/default/files/core/white-paper/CORE_PA_Pilot_Issue_Brief_v7.pdf))
- **Denial rate.** MA insurers denied **7.4% of requests in 2022 and 6.4% in 2023** in whole or in part. ([KFF 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-plans-denied-a-larger-share-of-prior-authorization-requests-in-2022-than-in-prior-years/), [AHA on KFF 2023](https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2025-01-29-kff-ma-insurers-made-nearly-50-million-prior-authorization-determinations-2023))
- **Appeal rate.** Only **about 10 to 12% of denials are appealed** (9.9% in 2022, 11.7% in 2023). ([KFF 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-plans-denied-a-larger-share-of-prior-authorization-requests-in-2022-than-in-prior-years/), [AHA on KFF 2023](https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2025-01-29-kff-ma-insurers-made-nearly-50-million-prior-authorization-determinations-2023))
- **Overturn on appeal.** When providers do appeal, **over 80% of denials are overturned** (83.2% in 2022). The gap between a 6 to 7% denial rate, a 10% appeal rate and an 80%+ overturn rate is the core waste: most denials stand only because nobody fights them. ([KFF 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-plans-denied-a-larger-share-of-prior-authorization-requests-in-2022-than-in-prior-years/), [AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/over-80-prior-auth-appeals-succeed-why-aren-t-there-more))
- **Wrongful denials.** HHS OIG found **13% of MA prior-auth denials met Medicare coverage rules** and should have been approved, plus 18% of payment denials. ([HHS OIG OEI-09-18-00260](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2022/some-medicare-advantage-organization-denials-of-prior-authorization-requests-raise-concerns-about-beneficiary-access-to-medically-necessary-care/))
- **Cost of a denial.** Providers spend an average of **$43.84 to fight one denied claim**, about **$19.7 billion a year** in total denial-management expense. Reworking a single denied claim runs $25 and up. ([Premier](https://premierinc.com/newsroom/blog/trend-alert-private-payers-retain-profits-by-refusing-or-delaying-legitimate-medical-claims), [Becker's](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/finance/claims-denials-are-costing-hospitals-nearly-20b-per-year/))

### The buyer

PriorProof sells to whoever eats the prior-auth labor cost today.

- **Specialty practices** with high prior-auth load (oncology, cardiology, orthopedics, rheumatology, gastroenterology, radiology). These feel the 13-hours-a-week pain hardest and often staff a dedicated prior-auth person.
- **Revenue-cycle-management (RCM) firms** that run prior auth and denials for many practices. They buy volume and resell the time savings as margin.
- **Medical billing companies** that already hold the payer relationships and the charts.
- **Group practices and small hospital systems** with a central authorizations team.

The economic buyer is the practice administrator or the RCM operations lead. The budget already exists as salaried staff time, so this is a cost-substitution sale, not a net-new line item.

### Pricing

Three tiers. The flat per-packet price undercuts the loaded cost of a manual prior auth and sits near the narrow CAQH labor figure, so the ROI reads at a glance.

- **Pay as you go: $12 per completed packet.** No commitment. For small or occasional users. This is roughly half the low end of the loaded manual cost ($25 to $90) and about a quarter of the $43.84 it costs just to fight one denial.
- **Pro: $349 per seat per month**, includes 50 packets, then $7 per packet. For specialty practices and billing clerks with steady volume.
- **Scale: custom, $5 to $7 per packet** on an annual commit, with BAA, SSO and audit logs. For RCM and billing companies.

Across the mix the **blended realized price is about $9 per packet**. The defensible anchor: even the narrow CAQH labor cost is about $11 per manual prior auth, and the loaded cost is $25 to $90, so a $9 to $12 finished packet saves the buyer money on the direct-labor basis alone and much more once rework and denials are counted.

### COGS

Variable cost is dominated by LLM spend. The flow is: parse the policy into criteria, locate candidate chart spans per criterion, prove or refuse each criterion against a cited span, then assemble the packet.

Per-packet model assumptions:
- About **10 criteria per policy**, a few calls each (locate, prove, format), plus about 5 assembly calls. Call it **~35 model calls per packet**.
- Shared context (policy plus relevant chart, about 23k tokens) is cached once and read cheaply on later calls. Prompt caching reads at about 0.1x the input rate, which is what makes this viable.
- Per packet that works out to roughly **300k cached-read input tokens, 35k fresh input tokens and 20k output tokens**.

On a mid-tier frontier model as the reference (Claude Sonnet 5 list price $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output, cache reads at 0.1x), the arithmetic is about **$0.48 per packet**. Rounding up for retries, longer charts and a QA pass gives a planning number of **about $0.60 per packet**. A cheaper model for the extraction subcalls (Haiku-class at $1 / $5 per million) pulls it toward $0.20. A top-tier model throughout (Opus-class at $5 / $25) pushes it to about $1.20. ([Anthropic pricing](https://www.anthropic.com/pricing))

- **Hosting on Vercel: roughly $20 to $150 per month**, mostly fixed. Vercel Pro starts at about $20 per member per month plus usage. Serverless function compute per packet is a few cents.
- **Other fixed infra:** a Postgres database (Neon or Vercel Postgres), error monitoring, domain and email. Call it **$150 to $300 per month all-in for a solo founder** including Vercel.
- **Payment processing:** about 3% on card revenue, folded into the tier economics.

Planning figure: **variable cost ~$0.60 per packet**, fixed infra **~$200 per month**.

### Gross margin and unit economics

- Blended price per packet: **$9.00**
- Variable cost per packet: **$0.60**
- **Contribution per packet: $8.40**
- **Gross margin: about 93%**

This is standard AI-application economics. The product is labor it replaces at near-zero marginal cost.

### Break-even

- **Infra-only break-even: about 25 packets per month** ($200 fixed divided by $8.40 contribution). This is trivially cleared by a single pilot.
- **Break-even including a $3,000 per month founder draw: about 380 packets per month** ($3,200 divided by $8.40).

For scale: one five-physician specialty group generates about **840 prior authorizations per month** (39 per physician per week times 5, times 4.33 weeks). So a single mid-size group, even at partial adoption, covers the founder's salary and the infra several times over.

### The value anchor

What the buyer gets per packet, in the real figures:

- **Time reclaimed: about 20 minutes of clinician and staff time per request** (13 hours per week over about 39 requests). PriorProof returns a finished, cited packet, so it gives back most of that 20 minutes.
- **Direct cost undercut:** a manual prior auth costs the provider about **$11** in CAQH labor terms and **$25 to $90 loaded**. A $9 to $12 packet is cheaper than the keystrokes on the narrow number and a fraction of the loaded cost.
- **Denials avoided:** 6 to 7% of MA requests are denied, and a large share of those are missing-documentation denials. A criterion-complete, span-cited submission attacks exactly that class. When a denial still lands, over 80% of appeals win, yet only about 10% get appealed because appeals cost $43.84 each to fight. PriorProof's cited spans and named gaps make both the first submission and any appeal cheap to produce, which is where the recoverable money sits.
- **Wrongful-denial recovery:** HHS OIG found 13% of MA denials were actually wrong. An evidence-complete packet is the lever that turns those into overturns instead of write-offs.

The one-line pitch: **PriorProof turns 20 minutes of clinician time and an $11 to $90 manual task into a $9 cited packet, and it makes the 80% of appeals that win cheap enough to actually file.**

### Compliance note (affects cost and ramp)

PriorProof handles PHI, so HIPAA applies and a signed BAA is required with every subprocessor that touches charts: the hosting provider and the LLM vendor. This is standard for enterprise tiers of Vercel and the major model providers, but it adds onboarding friction and is the main reason the sales ramp lags a consumer SaaS curve. ## 1. Install the CLI (confirmed from docs)

Linux (your platform) and the general-purpose path:
```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
# nightly channel: curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly
entire version   # verify
```

macOS alternative (Homebrew 6.0.10+):
```bash
brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire
```

From Go source (needs Go 1.27.1+, this is the only path that needs Go; packaged installs bundle their own runtime):
```bash
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/git-remote-entire@latest
export PATH="$HOME/go/bin:$PATH"
```

The CLI is MIT-licensed and open source (repo github.com/entireio/cli).

Prerequisites (confirmed): Git installed and configured; a GitHub account with an accessible repo; an AI coding agent installed (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.); macOS/Linux/Windows. Optional: the `gh` CLI if you want to create a demo repo from the terminal. A C compiler is NOT required for the standard prebuilt installs; the hackathon page mentions a C compiler only for building Brain/Graph tree-sitter bindings from source, which you avoid by using the prebuilt installers.

Important mechanism (confirmed): Entire works by installing git hooks plus agent hooks in your repo. It captures your AI coding-agent SESSION and links it to a git COMMIT. That pairing is a checkpoint. This is a development-time tool that records how the code was built; it is not a runtime state store for your own deployed agent (this matters for your PriorProof design, see section 5).

## 2. Authenticate and connect GitHub

### Interactive vs headless (confirmed from the CLI README)

Login command: `entire login`.

## 5. Using checkpoints meaningfully in PriorProof (important correction)

Your example "checkpoint the parsed chart after extraction and the coverage state before packet assembly, so a run resumes without re-reading the chart" describes runtime state-snapshotting of the deployed prior-auth agent. Entire does not do that. Entire checkpoints are development-time pairings of a coding-agent session with a git commit. It will not natively snapshot your Next.js app's execution state on Vercel. State that plainly in planning so the submission narrative stays honest.

Two clean ways to make the idea real and still win "Best Use of Entire":

- Map each pipeline stage to its own checkpoint during the build. Build chart-extraction, coverage-lookup, and packet-assembly each in a dedicated agent session and commit each as its own checkpoint with a descriptive message. A judge then runs `entire checkpoint explain <ID>` or opens the commit URL and sees the reasoning, prompts, and diffs behind each stage. This is the most direct, confirmed, meaningful use, and it is exactly what the checkpoint link in the submission should showcase. Pair it with Graph (so the agent navigates the growing codebase cheaply) and Brain (persist decisions like "coverage rules live in X, prove-or-refuse threshold is Y" via `entire brain remember`, recalled in later sessions). Using all three is the strongest claim for the prize.
- Implement the runtime resume as a PriorProof app feature in its own right (write parsed-chart JSON and coverage state to disk or a store, resume from there), which is good engineering independent of Entire. If you want an Entire angle on the actual agent run, Entire's confirmed resume primitive is cross-session, not cross-request: `entire session resume` / Resume Sessions continues a stopped coding session or hands work between agents. Tell the "resume without re-reading the chart" story as your app feature; do not attribute it to Entire checkpoints.

Submission pointer (confirmed): neatHack requires an accessible checkpoint link + ID. Use the checkpoint for your most illustrative stage commit (for example the coverage/packet-assembly commit), give its entire.io/gh/... URL and its `Entire-Checkpoint:` ULID.

## PriorProof × neatlogs: TypeScript/Node instrumentation

### 1. Package name and version (CONFIRMED)

- npm package: **`neatlogs`** (unscoped). Current version **1.1.28**, license MIT, `engines.node >=18.0.0`.
- Source repo: **github.com/neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript** (the npm `neatlogs` package IS this TS SDK; the Python SDK is a separate `neatlogs` on PyPI).
- It is **OpenTelemetry-native** (depends on `@opentelemetry/*` and `protobufjs`); it exports OTLP-proto spans over HTTP.
- Related package: `@neatlogs/wizard` (v0.1.11), the `npx @neatlogs/wizard` auto-setup CLI. Not needed if you instrument by hand.

```bash
npm install neatlogs
```

Sources: [neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript README](https://github.com/neatlogs/neatlogs-typescript) · npm registry `registry.npmjs.org/neatlogs` (dist-tags.latest = 1.1.28) · [hackathon setup guide](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/neatlogs-setup-guide.html).

### 2. Initialization (CONFIRMED)

- Env var: **`NEATLOGS_API_KEY`**. There is **no project id for the SDK** — the API key itself selects the project.
- Two keys exist in the dashboard and they are not interchangeable: use the **Project API key** (the top one) for the Node SDK. The **HTTP ingest key starting with `nlw_`** is for raw HTTP / the browser SDK only; passing `nlw_` to the Node SDK returns 401. (`NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` + `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` exist only for reading traces back via the CLI/public API, not for ingest.)

```typescript
import { init, shutdown, wrapOpenAI } from 'neatlogs';
import OpenAI from 'openai';

await init({ apiKey: process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY, workflowName: 'my-first-app' });
const client = wrapOpenAI(new OpenAI());
// ...
await shutdown(); // flushes anything still queued
```

Key `init()` options (from the README `InitOptions` table): `apiKey` (default `process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY`, export disabled if unset), `workflowName`, `userId`, `tags`, `metadata`, `debug`, `disableExport`, `sampleRate`, `captureLogs` (needed for `log()`), `endpoint` (default `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`; SDK posts to `/v1/traces` and `/v1/logs`), `registerShutdownHandlers` (default true). Ingest uses header `x-api-key` + gzip (confirmed in `src/core/client.ts`). Must be wrapped in an `async function main()`; no top-level await.

### 3. Trace for one run + spans per step (CONFIRMED)
